Accordingly, the disclosure and the figures are to be regarded as illustrative rather than restrictive.
[0020] Embodiments of the present invention disclose a brick composition. 
[0021] One of the major environmental concerns is the management of MSWI ash, a byproduct generated from waste-to-energy plants. MSWI ash contains valuable mineral components such as silica, alumina, and calcium, which can be repurposed for construction applications.
[0022] Managing Municipal Solid Waste Incinerator (MSWI) ash is a crucial task to ensure environmental safety and sustainability. The ash contains various constituents, some of which may be hazardous, like heavy metals or dioxins. Proper management involves treating, recycling, or safely disposing of the ash.
[0023] MSWI ash typically consists of bottom ash, fly ash, and air pollution control residues. MSWIA collected from the incineration plants and utilised for construction purposes enables the ash to be diverted from landfills and to reduce the carbon footprint overall.
[0024] In the present invention MSWIA is collected from the incineration plants and explored for its possible use in construction industry by preparing a brick. The MSWIA obtained from the incineration plants have already undergone required pre-treatment, which ensures their suitability in further utilisation. Typically, the MSWIA of the present invention does not contain any heavy metals or hazardous elements.
[0025] To enhance the properties of MSWI ash-based bricks, zeolite nanoparticles offer a promising solution. Zeolites are crystalline aluminosilicate materials known for their high surface area, adsorption capacity, and ion-exchange properties. When incorporated into brick formulations, zeolite nanoparticles improve mechanical strength, thermal insulation, and water resistance while also helping to stabilize heavy metals present in MSWI ash, reducing environmental risks.
[0026] In the present invention, MSWIA was incorporated in a brick formulation by mixing it with clay and zeolite in varying proportions. The following table will identify the varying proportions tried and tested for the purposes of the present invention.

[0028] Clay, MSWIA, and zeolite nanoparticles are mixed in different proportions to check the optimum mix proportion. Water is added, and the mixture is kneaded until it becomes homogeneous and then moulded into brick shapes using compression. 
[0029] After that, bricks are air-dried for 24 hours to reduce moisture content. Bricks are fired at high temperature to achieve optimal strength and durability. The bricks are cooled gradually and tested for strength, water absorption, and other properties. 
[0030] In a preferred embodiment, the dimension of bricks was kept at 23.5 cm length, 11.5 cm width, and 8 cm height as depicted in figure 1.
[0031] It is observed from Table 1 that the addition of MSWI ash at 20% had the lowest density and lower water absorption rate. In contrast, the sample containing 20% MSWIA had the highest compressive strength.
[0032] It is further observed that as the proportion of the MSWIA varies, the compressive strength also varies, but which is always observed to be lesser than the sample containing 20% MSWIA. 
[0033] The optimum result is obtained by mixing of 75% clay, 20% MSWI ash, and 5% of zeolite nanoparticles. The experimental results shows that the compressive strength of bricks is 12.5 MPa, water absorption 11%, and density is 1780 kg/m3.
[0034] The usage of MSWIA improves thermal insulation, and reduces the weight of bricks, but a higher content of MSWI ash can lower strength and durability. Zeolite enhances strength, durability, and water resistance, making it a better alternative for structural applications. It is added 5% with the different proportion of clay and MSWI ash to obtain an optimum mix design. A balanced mix of MSWI ash and zeolite makes the brick with good strength, insulation, and weather resistance, making it ideal for sustainable construction.
[0035] Incorporating Municipal Solid Waste Incineration Ash (MSWIA) into brick formulations can enhance their thermal insulation properties. This improvement is largely due to the porous nature of the ash, which increases the brick's ability to reduce heat transfer. The added porosity introduces air pockets within the brick structure, acting as thermal barriers and thereby decreasing thermal conductivity
[0036] The production of bricks using clay, MSWI ash, and zeolite nanoparticles enhances sustainability while improving mechanical and durability properties. This mix reduces the environmental impact by incorporating waste materials while maintaining or even improving the performance of traditional clay bricks. The addition of zeolite nanoparticles enhances strength, durability, and adsorption properties, making the bricks more resistant to environmental degradation.
[0037] This approach not only reduces dependency on virgin raw materials but also utilizes waste streams effectively, aligning with circular economy principles. The resulting light weight bricks offer improved compressive strength, better thermal efficiency, enhanced durability, and eco-friendly characteristics, making them an ideal choice for sustainable construction, affordable housing, and resilient infrastructure.
[0038] By integrating advanced nanotechnology with waste valorisation strategies, the present invention addresses key challenges in the construction sector, providing a cost-effective, sustainable, and innovative alternative to conventional building materials while contributing to global environmental conservation efforts.

Dietary habits have increasingly favored processed, high-calorie meals, contributing to the prevalence of lifestyle-related diseases such as diabetes, heart disease, and obesity. Traditional cookies lack essential nutrients, bioactive compounds, and antioxidants. The butterfly pea extract, rich in anthocyanins, offers anti-inflammatory, anti-diabetic, and cardiovascular benefits. However, its application in widely consumed baked goods remains unexplored. This invention integrates multigrain formulations, including ragi, wheat, and gram flour, with butterfly pea extract to develop a nutritious and appealing alternative to conventional snacks. 
While cookies cover a broad spectrum of baked good, their versatility and ability to accommodate so many different add-ins is what makes them a widely beloved treat. Functional ingredients, characterized are active components of food that promote the health of individual/s or population as a whole when taken in adequate quantity, include ragi (finger millet), whole wheat, oats, almond, pistachios, cashew and raisins that can replacements for all-purpose flour too, chia seeds and butterfly pea extract extracts which can not only provide nutrition but also the sensory embellishment associated with cookies without affecting palatability.
The idea is to manufacture a tasty, nutrient-dense cookie that incorporates both modern and traditional superfoods to support wellbeing. The product attempts to provide a healthy snacking option that is high in fiber, protein, vital vitamins, and antioxidants by blending finger millet, whole wheat, oats, almonds, pistachios, cashews, raisins, chia seeds, and butterfly pea extract extracts. These cookies appeal to consumers who are health-conscious since they offer practical advantages like better digestion, longer-lasting energy, and increased immunity while still tasting great and looking good. The cookies are prepared with carefully selected ingredients to ensure taste, and nutrition. The base is a mix of ragi, whole wheat and oats that lends you the complex carbs and nutritional fiber. Ragi, or finger millet, finely ground for smooth texture and a calcium bonus. Sweetened naturally and softened by pre-soaking, raisins are a great supplement with depth of flavor to balance out chopped or crushed cashews, pistachios and almonds to add pleasing crunch. Butterfly pea extract are incorporated for their bright natural colors and antioxidant properties, and chia seeds serve as a nutrient-dense binding agent by providing omega-3 fatty acids along with a light texture. The recipe uses natural sweeteners such as jaggery to keep the sugar count down, while balancing wet and dry ingredients to create a cookie that is chewy on the inside, crispy at the surface. Superfoods are distributed evenly thanks to uniform kneading, which also avoids segregation. A flawlessly cooked, nutrient-rich cookie is the result of carefully controlling the baking process at 160–180°C to maintain nutritional integrity and provide an enticing golden-brown finish. Adjustments are made to account for the moisture from raisins and extracts.

Cake has its roots in ancient cultures, when its earliest iterations were more akin to sweet breads prepared with honey, nuts, and fruits. Early cake recipes are attributed to the ancient Egyptians, who frequently used yeast as a leavening agent. Cake recipes improved over the ages, particularly during the Renaissance when cakes began to use sugar and spices. The variety of cakes we know today is the result of improvements in baking technologies that made cakes more widely available by the 19th century. Regular cakes do have certain drawbacks, though, especially if they contain a lot of sugar and refined wheat. They contain a lot of sugar, which when consumed in excess can lead to weight gain, diabetes, and other health problems. Furthermore, the refined flour used in many cakes is deficient in fibre and vital nutrients, which causes blood sugar levels to rise quickly and only gives you short-term energy. The risk of heart disease can also be raised by cakes that contain unhealthy fats, such as trans fats found in some oils. On the other hand, there are certain health advantages to turmeric cake, which is prepared using milk, turmeric, refined flour, powdered sugar, and baking powder. Curcumin, an antioxidant and anti-inflammatory compound found in turmeric, may help prevent chronic illnesses and lessen inflammation. Calcium, protein, and vital vitamins for healthy bones and muscles are all found in milk. Because of turmeric's health benefits, turmeric cakes are a healthier option than typical cakes.
Turmeric includes curcumin, a substance with potent anti-inflammatory qualities, a cake made with turmeric, egg, powdered sugar, and baking powder can have a number of health advantages. Numerous illnesses, including cardiovascular disease, arthritis, and even some forms of cancer, are associated with chronic inflammation. . Turmeric's anti-inflammatory properties can be easily included into your diet by using it in cake form, which may help lower the body's general level of inflammation. Another important component that provides a multitude of vital nutrients is eggs. They are abundant in high-quality protein, which aids in immune system function, muscle regeneration, and other body functions. Eggs also include vitamins B12, D, and choline, which are essential for bone strength, energy metabolism, and brain function. Although it has no direct nutritional advantages, the baking powder is crucial to the texture of the cake since it helps it rise during baking, giving it a light and airy appearance. However, because the cake contains powdered sugar, it still contains refined sugar, which, if consumed in excess, can cause blood sugar increases and weight gain. Although sugar must be added for sweetness, excessive usage of it may negate some of the possible health advantages. One may use natural sweeteners like honey or maple syrup or cut back on the sugar to make this turmeric cake even healthier. Furthermore, using whole grain flour instead of refined flour would boost the cake's fiber level and make it a more well-rounded choice. It's crucial to keep in mind that this cake is still a dessert and that its sugar and refined flour content should be consumed in moderation to maintain a balanced diet, even though it offers a special combination of anti-inflammatory properties from turmeric and nutritional support from eggs.
Made with eggs, butter, powdered sugar, maida (refined flour), and baking powder, a turmeric cake can have a delightfully rich and soft texture and appearance. The eggs help to create a moist, silky crumb by binding the components together and giving them structure. A velvety, rich texture is added by the butter, which also gives the cake a soft, melt-in-your-mouth texture and enhances the flavour with its creamy undertones. The cake is light and not too dense because of the powdered sugar's smooth, delicately textured sweetness.
Although maida (refined flour) may not have the bulk or fibre content of whole grain substitutes, it produces a soft, fine crumb with a delicate feel. In addition to giving the cake a lightness that delightfully contrasts with the richness of the butter and eggs, the baking powder aids in the cake's rising and gives it an airy, fluffy texture.
Turmeric gives the cake a delicate earthy flavour and a golden yellow colour, which enhances its appearance and makes it seem welcoming. The warm, comforting aroma that the turmeric produces when baked goes well with the cake's moist, soft inside. Even though the cake is soft and fragile, it slices easily since it maintains its shape nicely.
All things considered, this turmeric cake is rich and cozy due to its buttery texture, which is light, moist, and fluffy. It is a pleasure in flavour and presentation because of its vivid colour and even, smooth crumb structure, which enhance its visual and sensual appeal.

The present invention relates to a nutritious multigrain cookie formulation enriched with hibiscus extract, designed to provide enhanced antioxidant, fiber, and protein content while maintaining sensory appeal. The cookie is prepared using a functional blend of ragi, whole wheat, oats, almonds, pistachios, cashews, chia seeds, raisins, and hibiscus extract, ensuring a healthier alternative to conventional snacks. Hibiscus extract serves as a natural source of anthocyanins and antioxidants, offering anti-inflammatory, cardiovascular, and metabolic health benefits. The formulation replaces refined sugar with jaggery, making it diabetic-friendly and heart-healthy, while eliminating preservatives, artificial additives, and refined flour. The baking process is optimized at 160°C to preserve nutritional integrity and achieve a balanced texture. This invention provides a functional, sustainable, and health-conscious snacking option suitable for individuals seeking nutrient-dense, wholesome food choices.

Dietary habits have transitioned towards processed, high-calorie foods, contributing to lifestyle diseases like obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disorders. Traditional cookies lack essential nutrients, fiber, antioxidants, and bioactive compounds.
Hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa) is a potent source of anthocyanins, antioxidants, and bioactive phytochemicals known for their anti-inflammatory, antidiabetic, and cardiovascular health benefits. Despite its well-documented health advantages, hibiscus is rarely incorporated in widely consumed snacks like cookies.
Multigrain formulations including ragi, wheat, and gram flour provide a good source of fiber, micronutrients, and plant-based proteins, addressing common nutritional deficiencies in snack foods. The main challenge lies in achieving an optimal balance of taste, texture, and nutritional composition while ensuring consumer acceptability.
Cookies are a widely popular baked product known for their versatility and adaptability to various ingredients. Incorporating functional ingredients like ragi (finger millet), whole wheat, oats, almond, pistachios, cashew, raisins, chia seeds, hibiscus extracts can enhance the nutritional and sensory properties of cookies, making them healthier alternatives while maintaining palatability.
The concepts are to create a delicious, nutrient-rich cookie with modern and old superfoods to nourish wellbeing. It claims to be a high fiber, high protein, vital vitamins and antioxidants rich healthy snacking and have a blend of ragi (finger millet), whole wheat, oats, almonds, pistachios, cashews, raisins, chia seeds and hibiscus extracts. These cookies appeal to consumers who are health-conscious since they offer practical advantages like better digestion, longer-lasting energy, and increased immunity while still tasting great and looking good. The cookies are made with a curated blend of ingredients to ensure a portion that is delicious as well as nutritious. Base is basically ragi, whole wheat, oats, which comprises of complex carbs and nutritional fibre. A smooth texture and a calcium boost are what finely ground ragi adds to it. Raisins that have been soaked in water give the dish natural sweetness and softness, while chopped or crushed cashews, pistachios, and almonds add a delightful crunch as well as depth of flavour. Hibiscus extracts are included, for their deep natural colours and antioxidant properties, and chia seeds as a nutrient-rich binding agent, contributing omega-3 fatty acids and a light texture. The recipe uses natural sweeteners such as jaggery to maintain low sugar levels, and balances wet and dry ingredients to create a cookie that’s somewhat chewy on the inside and crunchy on the outside. Superfoods are distributed evenly thanks to uniform kneading, which also avoids segregation. A flawlessly cooked, nutrient-rich cookie is the result of carefully controlling the baking process at 160° C to maintain nutritional integrity and provide an enticing golden-brown finish. Adjustments are made to account for the moisture from raisins and extracts.

The present invention relates to the development of a gluten-free, high-protein bar utilizing Bauhinia vahlii seeds as a novel plant-based protein source. Bauhinia vahlii seeds are rich in protein (20-25%), essential amino acids, dietary fiber, and minerals. However, their utilization in food products has been limited due to the presence of antinutritional factors (ANFs) such as tannins, phytates, and trypsin inhibitors. The developed protein bar is gluten-free, sugar-free, and free from artificial additives, making it suitable for individuals with gluten intolerance, celiac disease, and those seeking plant-based protein alternatives. Additionally, this innovation promotes sustainability by utilizing an underexplored protein source and provides economic benefits to local communities engaged in seed collection and processing.

The present invention relates to a novel plant-based protein source for the development of gluten-free and high-protein food products. Specifically, it pertains to the formulation and processing of Bauhinia vahlii seeds to create a high-protein, gluten-free, and sugar-free energy bar.

With the increasing prevalence of gluten intolerance and celiac disease, there is a growing demand for alternative sources of high-protein and allergen-free nutrition. Conventional protein bars are typically made using whey, wheat, and soy protein powders, often containing high amounts of refined sugar, artificial additives, and preservatives, reducing their overall health benefits.
Bauhinia vahlii seeds have been identified as an excellent plant-based protein source, containing approximately 20-25% protein, including essential amino acids such as lysine and arginine. They are also rich in dietary fiber and essential minerals like calcium, iron, and magnesium. However, their use in food formulation is limited due to the presence of antinutritional factors (ANFs). This invention aims to develop a gluten-free, sugar-free, high-protein bar by optimizing processing techniques to remove ANFs while retaining nutritional benefits. 
The primary objective of this invention is to provide a plant-based protein alternative for health-conscious consumers, particularly those with gluten intolerance or celiac disease. The formulation of the bar avoids common allergens like gluten, dairy, and soy while offering high protein content with natural sweeteners and binding agents. TECHNICAL FIELD 
[0001] The present disclosure relates to an automated data acquisition and processing in industrial environments, particularly in the context Industry 4.0 applications involving non-intrusive, vision-based systems, targeting non-intrusive, non-contact methods of acquiring data from various display devices, such as 7-segment displays, analog gauges, and machine-mounted indicators.  BACKGROUND
[0002] In traditional manufacturing and industrial environments, data acquisition from machines is typically achieved through sensor-based systems that are installed directly onto machinery. However, this approach is often problematic, especially in environments where retrofitting existing machines with sensors is impractical, costly, or disruptive to operations. Legacy machines, which may lack digital interfaces or IoT compatibility, require specialized adaptations for sensor integration, further increasing costs and complicating system maintenance. Additionally, sensor-based solutions can be difficult to scale across large industrial spaces where numerous machines and varied types of data need to be captured, leading to logistical and network challenges.
[0003] In industrial environments, effective monitoring and data acquisition from machinery are crucial for optimizing performance, predicting maintenance needs, and minimizing downtime. Traditionally, data from machines are gathered through physical sensors attached to various machine components, but this approach has significant limitations. First, retrofitting machines with sensors can be prohibitively expensive and labour-intensive, particularly for legacy equipment not designed for digital integration. Sensors also suffer from wear and tear over time, requiring frequent maintenance, recalibration, and replacement, leading to increased costs and operational interruptions. Additionally, sensor-based systems often lack flexibility; each sensor is typically designed to measure a single parameter, necessitating multiple sensors to monitor all relevant metrics, which complicates system architecture and further increases costs.
[0004] Further, physical sensor deployments are highly sensitive to precise placement, and even a minor displacement of a few millimeters whether during installation or over time due to machine usage, vibrations, or environmental factors can cause the sensor to fall outside its defined tolerances. This slight misalignment can significantly impact performance, potentially rendering the sensor ineffective or compromising the accuracy of the data it collects.
[0005] In cases where sensors cannot be used such as when machines operate in hazardous environments or in situations requiring precise non-contact measurements reliable alternatives are scarce. Even when sensors are feasible, transmitting data from numerous devices can strain network bandwidth and limit real-time responsiveness, especially when remote or large-scale monitoring is involved. Further, traditional methods of analyzing and processing this data are often unable to detect nuanced patterns or anomalies that may signal underlying issues in machine performance. The present disclosure overcomes these problems by using image capturing devices to read display values directly from existing gauges and screens, enabling a sensor less data acquisition approach. This solution integrates edge computing and machine learning for localized processing, OCR for data extraction from images, and scalable network protocols for efficient data transfer. Together, these advancements enable a more resilient, cost-effective, and versatile solution for monitoring complex industrial environments.
[0006] Another important use case arises when the machine in question performs complex and variable movements such as in a multi-axis CNC machine where fixed sensor placements may not be feasible or reliable across different machine configurations or product variations. In such scenarios, the dynamic nature of the operations means that a sensor positioned optimally for one setup may be misaligned or obstructed in another, leading to inconsistent performance or the need for frequent recalibration and repositioning.
[0007] Conventional methods for industrial data acquisition largely rely on direct sensor integration, where various physical sensors are attached to machinery to monitor parameters like temperature, pressure, speed, and voltage. These sensors can be effective in capturing specific data points, but they come with several drawbacks. For one, the installation and retrofitting of sensors are both time-consuming and expensive, particularly for older machines not originally designed to support them. Each parameter requires a dedicated sensor, making the approach both costly and complex when multiple parameters need monitoring. Moreover, sensors are prone to wear and degradation, leading to frequent recalibration and maintenance demands, which can interrupt production and increase costs. In cases where sensors are exposed to harsh conditions such as high temperatures, vibrations, or corrosive environments their lifespan is further reduced, requiring even more frequent replacements.
[0008] Another limitation of conventional sensor-based systems is their dependence on wired connections, which can complicate installation and hinder flexibility, or on wireless technologies like Wi-Fi, which may lack the robustness needed for large-scale industrial applications. Furthermore, sensor-based systems typically generate vast amounts of raw data that require extensive processing to extract meaningful insights. This data often overloads communication networks and incurs latency issues, limiting real-time monitoring capabilities. Some advanced systems incorporate IoT frameworks for better connectivity, but even these can struggle with network congestion, security vulnerabilities, and limited scalability. While newer digital solutions, such as SCADA (Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition) systems, address some connectivity and real-time data visualization challenges, they still depend on extensive sensor networks and may be financially impractical for smaller enterprises. 
[0009] Further limitations and disadvantages of conventional and traditional approaches will become apparent to one of skill in the art, through comparison of described systems with some aspects of the present disclosure, as set forth in the remainder of the present application and with reference to the drawings.

[0022] The present disclosure provides a non-intrusive, automated data acquisition system designed to capture and process real-time operational data from industrial machines without the need for direct sensor integration. This system employs strategically mounted image capturing devices that focus on machine displays, such as 7-segment displays, analog gauges, and digital screens, to extract critical parameters related to machine performance. Upon powering up, each image capturing device transmits a "birth message" to a local server, containing identification details and configuration parameters. The server responds by instructing the devices to capture images at predefined intervals from specified regions of interest on display. These captured images are then locally stored and processed to extract data values, utilizing techniques such as optical character recognition (OCR), noise reduction, segmentation, colour identification, shape identification, object identification, distance assessment, size assessment, and contrast enhancement to ensure high accuracy even under challenging lighting conditions.
[0023] The system also incorporates edge computing capabilities, allowing for preliminary data processing and anomaly detection directly at the image capturing device, which reduces network bandwidth usage and latency. Anomalies or unusual readings trigger the capture of additional images, which are sent to the local server for further analysis. Data processed on the local server is structured and transmitted to a remote server, where it can be viewed on a dashboard or further integrated with advanced tools, such as augmented reality (AR) displays, digital twin simulations, or blockchain for secure record-keeping. Also, data processed on the local server has the benefit of extracting only required insights and inferences and leaving the original image within the site, as well as relieving the (small) camera devices from the responsibility of heavy computation, allowing them to operate efficiently, without needing more expensive equipment or computing platforms.
[0024] Additionally, the invention supports scalability by allowing remote servers to dynamically request images from multiple devices and integrates machine learning for predictive maintenance by analyzing historical data patterns. This system not only reduces dependency on physical sensors but also provides a robust, cost-effective, and scalable solution for real-time monitoring and remote management of industrial operations, advancing Industry 4.0 objectives across diverse industrial applications.

Traditional data acquisition methods, which often rely on physical sensors attached to each machine, are limited in flexibility, scalability, and compatibility with legacy equipment. These methods are also hindered by issues such as sensor wear, installation complexity, and high maintenance costs. The present disclosure overcomes these obstacles by using image capturing devices to monitor analog and digital displays on machines, enabling data collection without modifying or impacting the machine’s structure or operation. Additionally, present disclosure addresses challenges in managing large volumes of unstructured image data by implementing machine learning algorithms for anomaly detection, optical character recognition (OCR) for data extraction, and edge computing to process data locally, thus reducing latency and bandwidth requirements. This approach enhances data accessibility, accuracy, and timeliness, providing a scalable, low-cost solution suitable for diverse industrial applications, including predictive maintenance, remote monitoring, and real-time operational insights.

The server then sends instructions to the devices, specifying the exact regions on each display to monitor and setting image capture intervals to match the required data refresh rate for real-time monitoring.
[0067] At regular intervals, each image capturing device takes images of the specified regions on the machine displays. Edge computing capabilities on each device allow them to preprocess these images, including reducing noise, enhancing contrast, and detecting any anomalous readings using machine learning models. For example, if a hydraulic press’s temperature reading surpasses a critical threshold, the image capturing device detects this anomaly and captures additional images at higher frequency, transmitting them to the local server with a high-priority tag for immediate analysis. The local server performs further image processing, such as optical character recognition (OCR) to extract the numerical data from the display, and then structures this data into a message format that includes device ID, group ID, and timestamped data, which is sent to a remote server.
[0068] On the remote server, a dashboard presents real-time data updates, showing operators the performance metrics of each machine in the plant. In addition, the system enables operators to view historical data trends and receive predictive maintenance alerts when the system identifies patterns indicating potential equipment issues, such as consistently rising temperatures or pressure levels in certain machines. Using the dashboard’s augmented reality (AR) feature, operators can also visualize these metrics overlaid on virtual representations of the machines, facilitating faster decision-making and enhanced operational insight. The remote server further integrates with a digital twin platform, enabling the simulation of different operational scenarios and optimization of production workflows based on real-time and historical data. The secure storage of this data on a blockchain provides an additional layer of auditability and traceability, ensuring that the operational data remains unaltered and compliant with regulatory standards. This example illustrates how the disclosure seamlessly integrates advanced data acquisition, processing, and visualization technologies to deliver a comprehensive, scalable solution for industrial monitoring and management.
[0069] A detailed working example, in a large automotive manufacturing facility, the present disclosure is deployed to monitor the performance of five CNC machines, three hydraulic presses, and two conveyor systems spread across the production floor. Each machine has an image capturing device mounted approximately 12 inches from its display. The CNC machines feature 7-segment displays showing RPM, temperature, and cycle count, while the hydraulic presses and conveyor systems have analog gauges indicating pressure and load, respectively. Each image capturing device has an IP address and a unique device ID and is assigned to a group ID corresponding to the type of machine (e.g., CNC, hydraulic press, conveyor). Each device transmits a "birth message" to the local server, which contains its IP address, group ID, device ID, data type (e.g., RPM, temperature, pressure), and a capture interval of 5 seconds for CNCs and 10 seconds for presses and conveyors, based on optimal monitoring requirements, upon power-up.
[0070] The local server, after receiving the birth message, sends an instruction to each device to capture images every 5 or 10 seconds, depending on its assigned capture interval, and to focus on specific display regions. The image capturing devices use high-resolution sensors (e.g., 1080p) to ensure that display readings are clear, even under varying lighting conditions. Each device also uses edge computing to preprocess the images applying noise reduction and contrast enhancement to make the readings more legible. If, for instance, the temperature on a CNC machine rises above 120°C, as captured by an image and detected by an embedded machine learning model, the device takes three additional images in quick succession (every 1 second) and tags them as high-priority alerts, sending them directly to the local server for immediate analysis.
[0071] The local server performs optical character recognition (OCR) to accurately extract the temperature, RPM, and cycle count values, upon receiving the images, upon receiving the images. These extracted values are organized into a structured message format, which includes the timestamp, device ID, group ID, data type, and value (e.g., RPM: 1500, Temperature: 122°C, Cycle Count: 3050). This data is then forwarded to a remote server, where it can be visualized on a dashboard. The dashboard displays real-time metrics for each machine, with critical parameters highlighted. For instance, if a hydraulic press shows a pressure increase to 350 PSI, exceeding its operational limit of 300 PSI, the dashboard generates an alert with a timestamp, notifying the operator to inspect the machine.
[0072] The system also uses historical data to trigger predictive maintenance alerts. For example, the CNC machines' historical data shows that an RPM consistently over 2000 RPM for more than 10 minutes correlates with increased wear. When this condition is detected, the system recommends a maintenance check. The remote server is further configured to overlay real-time data on a digital twin model of the facility, enabling operators to view each machine’s status in a simulated production environment. Additionally, each captured data point is stored in a blockchain, ensuring that readings remain secure and auditable for regulatory compliance.
[0073] In this setup, the present disclosure not only provides continuous, sensor less monitoring but also generates actionable insights, including real-time alerts, predictive maintenance notifications, and secure data records, all of which contribute to a highly efficient, transparent, and optimized manufacturing operation.

Abstract:

This invention introduces a smart dumbbell designed to make strength training more efficient and hassle-free. Equipped with built-in motion sensors, including an accelerometer and a gyroscope, the dumbbell accurately tracks repetitions by analyzing movement patterns in real time. It ensures that only proper reps are counted while filtering out incorrect or incomplete motions. Users can set a target rep count before starting their workout, and once they reach their goal, a built-in buzzer sounds to notify them. This eliminates the need to manually track reps, allowing users to stay focused on their workout without distractions. Unlike other smart fitness devices, this dumbbell operates independently, requiring no mobile apps or external connections, making it simple and convenient for anyone to use.By automating rep counting and providing instant feedback, this smart dumbbell enhances workout effectiveness, keeps users motivated, and ensures a more structured training experience. Whether for casual fitness enthusiasts or serious athletes, it offers a practical solution to streamline strength training and reduce mental fatigue.

6) Detailed Description of the Preferred Embodiment: -
1. System Overview: The smart dumbbell system includes the following: Motion Sensors (Accelerometer & Gyroscope): Detects motion during exercise. Microcontroller Unit (MCU): Processes sensor data and defines the criteria for counting a repetition as correct. User Interface: The user can set rep goals through it. Audio Feedback System (Buzzer): The user is alerted by a sound signal to indicate reaching the set reps. Power Source: The unit is operated by a battery that can be recharged.
 2. Working Principle 
A. User Input: Stage The smart dumbbell system is turned on by the user. Then, the user chooses how many times he would like to repeat a single action, either by pressing buttons.
B. Motion Detection & Rep Counting: The accelerometer and gyroscope, on the other hand, are able to catch the movement that occurs when the user picks up or lowers the dumbbell. The microcontroller computes the movement pattern by referring to the key points (positions and speeds) of the tip of the dumbbell. Repeat counting is engaged only if the motion meets the predefined criteria (i.e., full range of motion).
C. Completion Check & Feedback: The system keeps checking and comparing the counted reps to the user’s target until the repetition target is reached. When all the reps are completed, a beep sound is produced by the buzzer to inform the user. Either the system is reinitialized for the next session or the user is asked to reset a new goal.

ABSTRACT SYSTEMS AND METHODS FOR PROVIDING MEDIA COMMUNICATION PROGRAMMABLE SERVICES Systems and methods for providing real-time media communication services to make use of a software application resident on a server that receives the media feeds of multiple sending participants, and generates a single composed media feed that includes media feeds of the sending participants and that sends the composed media feed to other computing services for manifold purposes like recording, re-broadcasting and/or re-transmission to remote computing devices of multiple real-time media communication participants. The composed media feed can include supplementary information in addition to the media feeds of live participants. This supplementary information is provided by means of API configurable programmatic code that is then executed and used as the software application resident on the server. Fig. 3

Description:BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

[0001] Figure 1 illustrates typical video conferencing and/or real-time media communications environments in which multiple sending connections (could be presenters, participants or could be any other source of media)

102, 104, 106 provide video feeds 102A, 104A, 106A to a server 108 that coordinates the media transmission. The server 108 could be a multipoint control unit (MCU) that connects different endpoints (e.g. receiving participants and/or sending presenters, or any combination of sending and/or receiving endpoints) providing appropriate media streams to all receiving endpoints. An MCU can perform video mixing, transcoding, security functions, as well as a range of other services. Most modern video communication services use a Selective Forwarding Unit (SFU) instead as a server 108, where media is selectively, packet by packet, forwarded from sending connections to receiving ones so that no need for mixing and/or transcoding is required. Packet selection for forwarding is based on a variety of strategies and smart decisions by the server to handle user quality of experience, quality of service, cost of operation, network usage, etc. Each endpoint, without loss of generality, can be connected by one or several network connections to the server. SFUs provide full flexibility to receiving endpoints to process individual media streams and arrange them as needed individually since each media stream is preserved independent (unlike on MCUs).

[ 0002 ] As illustrated in Figure 1a, in a typical state of the art real-time media communications environment, the service provides all of the individual media streams 102A, 104A, 106Ato each individual participant and/or

endpoint 110, 112, 114. This allows each endpoint 110, 112, 114 to arrange the media streams of the sending endpoints in any way that is deemed most helpful or convenient to a participant and/or receiving endpoint. This is common in real-time media communications, such as video conferencing, or even in near-real-time communications, where the media (e.g. video) feeds of each presenter and/or sender 102, 104, 106 are being seen essentially immediately by at least one of a participant and/or receiving endpoint. This ensures so-called interactive media communications. In a conferencing scenario, it allows participants to timely provide feedback, like posing questions to the presenting participants, and to interject as necessary such that the video conference closely resembles an in-person meeting. Figures 1 b & 1c depict how an endpoint typically hosts both sender & receiver. Any order or combination of senders and receivers into a given endpoint application could be considered. Figures 1 b & 1c depict examples of a real time communications system for the particular purpose of a video conferencing use case. At the same time, real-time media communications, and the scope of this disclosure, cover any other uses including applications of real-time media communications such as, but not limited to, social networking, e-learning, e-health, webinars, etc. Also, these can use any sort of communication topologies involving any combination of interactive low delay transmissions and delay-tolerant media transmissions, with diverse sending receiving participants topologies, from one or few sending participants to a very large number of receiving participants (e.g. 1:N or M:N, where N>M and even N»M), to a very large number of sending participants and few selective receiving participants (M:N where M>N and even M»N), while also even balanced N:N participant sessions, where the number of sending and receiving participants is equal. Sending and receiving participants may be the same participants, or distinct participants. Participant endpoints, may or may not be used by a subject. An endpoint may just be a programmatic application and/or destination service, or any other agent that consumes and/or generates media with its application for any purpose.

[0003] The price of the flexibility and scalability provided by an SFU server 108 is that it must send all media feeds for all of the sending participants 102, 104, 106 to each receiving participant, this places an increased processing cost on endpoints as well as on networking usage. At the same time, it places a much lower processing burden on the server 108, than an MCU would imply. On the other hand, if one can give up the flexibility, the cost of composing receiving views can be centralized in a single processing point like in MCUs (Figure 1c), having way more cost on the server, and spare communication and endpoint resources. Besides the server cost, the problems of the MCU, and the usual mixing and transcoding embedded in them is the lack of flexibility translated on a limited set of media composing and mixing preset and configurability available for choice.

[0004] It is common in different real-time media communication systems, to have services that receive one or many of the media streams being transmitted with the purpose of composing those or a part of them together to generate a unified output media stream. This is done by means of combining and mixing audio and/or video streams together. Being the purpose of this resulting composed stream of manifold possibilities. A list of those purposes, but not limited to are: recording, re-broadcasting using real-time interactive technologies, or delay tolerant such as HLS transmissions, or as a feed for a Media Gateway such as a custom-WebRTC-to-SIP interconnection Gateway, etc. These composing services are commonly limited to mixing the media feeds provided by sending participant endpoints. These media feeds being controllable through service APIs, as well as being possible to control by means of parametrized APIs the specific composing arrangement layout, inclusion and/or exclusion of media feeds, that in most complex services, the layout can be even specified by means of Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) descriptive code as seen and described in https://tokbox.com/developer/guides/archiving/layout-control.html and https://tokbox.com/developer/guides/archive-broadcast-layout/ .

[ 0005] During an actual media real-time communication (e.g. a video conference), it is common for a range of supplementary information to also be available to the presenters and/or participants and be part of the communication, as a component part of the application/s enabling the communication. The supplementary information can include, but not necessarily be limited to, at least one of a list of individuals that take part in the media communication session, the current status of participants, a dedicated window into which participants can type questions, text messaging windows, as well as a variety of additional information, and any other additional information rendered and displayed by the communications application. Often this supplementary information is presented around the edges of a participant’s display screen, with one or more video feeds of presenters or participants arranged in the center of the display screen. Any other arrangement layouts including all, or part of the participants media information together with all or part of any communications additional information and/or programmable media and/or visual effects are also possible as part of the presentation to a participant’s endpoint application display.

[0006] Furthermore, as mentioned above, when such a real-time media communication session is composed, with the exemplary purpose of being recorded, it is mostly the media feeds of the presenters that are being recorded. Supplementary information and/or visual effects are a de minimis part of the recording, and if some expression of those is present, are normally limited to a preset of options. This is a significant drawback, as there are times that the supplementary information forms a significant part of the overall communications experience, and/or additional arbitrary visual effects are desired in a recording and/or broadcast, that go beyond the possibilities of simple presset parameters, HTML and/or CSS.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS

[0018] The following detailed description of preferred embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings, which illustrate specific embodiments of the invention. Other embodiments having different structures and operations do not depart from the scope of the present invention.

[0019] Figure 2a illustrates a way of conducting a real-time media communications session where composed media feeds of all of the senders

are sent to each receiving participant. As shown in Figure 2a, the senders 202, 204, 206 send their respective media feeds 202A, 204A, 206A to a server 208. A first programmable Tenderer software application (PRSA) 220 on the server 208 then uses the sender video feeds 202A, 204A, 206A to generate a composed video feed 211 that includes the sender media feeds 202A, 204A, 206A. The composed video feed 211 may also include various items of supplementary information and media and visual effects. The first PRSA 220 then sends the composed video feed 211 to the computing devices of each of the participants 210, 212, 214, 216. Unlike composing in well known MCUs, in an embodiment of this invention composing is instead generated by means of a programmable Tenderer unit executing a software application provided as part of the control commands of the real-time media communications service (e.g. video conferencing).

[0020] Because the first PRSA 220 only needs to send a single composed video feed 211 to each participant, the first PRSA 220 requires less networking resources compared to the server 108 of a background art video conferencing system as illustrated in Figure 1. It can simultaneously provide a real-time full capacity of control of the composition, through programmatic means to the application embedded in the PRSA, without exceeding its processing and bandwidth limits.

[0021] In addition, if there is a need for multiple distinct rendered compositions to handle multiple parallel use cases it is possible for additional, PRSA units (e.g. 222) to also receive copies of the same sender video feeds 202A, 204A, 206A and to also generate a rendered composed media feed 211 that incorporates the sender video feeds 202A, 204A, 206A, as well as supplementary information and additional media effects. The additional PRSA 222 can then send the rendered composed media feed 211 to any further set

of receiving participants that may or may not include participants from the first PRSA.

[0022] In some embodiments, the PRSA units may be resident on the same server 208. In alternate embodiments, the PRSA units could be resident on one or more additional servers, containers, or virtualized machines, as depicted in the architecture of Figure 2b. Specifically, 1 -> N real-time communications can occur with multiple PRSA units (e.g. 224, 226) each deployed on their own servers, containers, or virtualized machines.

[0023] The real-time media communications system architecture illustrated in Figures 2.a and 2.b where one or more PRSAs receive and/or process multiple sender media feeds, generate a single rendered composed media feed, and send the single composed media feed to multiple real-time media communication participants, makes it possible to support the receipt of a large number of sending participants even on receiving endpoints and/or connections with very few resources available to them, as it is also known in the art of MCUs applications.

[0024] Figure 2.b shows an alternate method of conducting a real time media communications session where instead of the the PRSA (224, 226) sending a copy of the composed media stream to each receiver, it sends the stream once only to a Media SFU unit (228), the SFU then forwards the media stream to selected receivers. In some embodiments the PRSA unit (224, 226) will send multiple copies of the stream with different spatial and/or temporal characteristics to the SFU (228). The SFU can then forward the most appropriate version of the composed media stream to each receiver, thus enabling a better experience for the receiving endpoint (e.g. 210, 212, 214, 216) and making it possible to receive even on a low powered device by

electing to receive a smaller resolution or lower framerate version of the composed media stream coming from the PRSA unit(s).

[0025] In some embodiments a Recording Unit (230) with an associated Storage Unit (232) could be used to capture the composed media feed and store in the associated Storage Unit (232), which could be local or remote. This Recording Unit (230) could be embedded in a Receiver (216). In this case the Receiver (216), if network and computational resources allow, can request the highest quality version of the stream produced by the PRSA (e.g.

224) from the SFU (228) in order to record that on the integrated Recording Unit (230). Alternatively, the best possible quality following networking and/or computational resources would be recorded. In other embodiments the Recorder (230) and its storage unit (232) could be local to the PRSA (224) as shown in figure 2d. In this case the composed media stream is not required to be sent to the SFU (228) for forwarding to the Receivers (210, 212, 214, 216) for recording purposes but is instead routed to the Recording Unit (230) directly. Fig 2.c, 2.d and 2.e depict that PRSA composed media may just be used for specific uses within a session, while remote endpoints receive individual streams from the SFU for maximum flexible per-client experience. In another embodiment, rather than being integrated into a specific Receiver (216), the Recording Unit (230) is deployed on a dedicated server, container or virtual machine and receives the stream from the SFU (228) in a similar fashion to the other Receivers which receive streams (210, 212, 214, 216) as shown in figure 2.c. The composed stream from PRSA received by the recording unit may or may not be received by the endpoint receivers (210, 212, 214, 216), since it is possible endpoint receivers can leverage the capacity to receive individual streams for best flexibility if network resources allow, while PRSA composed stream is used within the real-time communications session for specific purposes like recording of a complex

composed experience, or other purposes like delay-tolerant broadcasting such as HLS transmissions, etc.

[0026] Figure 2d the recording Unit (230) could be using a specific stream received especially for the purpose of recording while the user of the Receiver (216) is viewing a different experience based on the individual streams forwarded by the SFU (228) from each of the senders (202, 204, 206), but not necessarily including the stream generated by the PRSA (224).

[0027] Figure 3 illustrates elements of the programmable renderer software application (PRSA) 300 that could be resident on a server 208 as illustrated in Figure 2 to perform the functions described above. Two embodiments are depicted as 300A and 300B respectively and the details of each are discussed in greater detail below.

[0028] The PRSA 300 includes a sender participant media feed receiving unit 308 that receives media feeds from multiple media communications sender participants. This could be accomplished by establishing a first media communications session between the PRSA 300 and the sender participants.

[0029] The PRSA 300 also includes a Composed Rendering Generation Unit 304 that programmatically mixes the sender media feeds and may also incorporate various items of supplementary information in the participant media feed based on information received from a supplementary information unit 310, as discussed below. The composed media feed may be then sent to each of the media communications participants.

[0030] In some embodiments, the PRSA 300 may be involved in a real-time media communications session with just the real-time media communications participants, in which the composed media feed is sent to the computing

devices of each of the real-time media communication participants. Various items of supplementary information may be sent from the participants to the PRSA 300 as part of that real-time media communications session, including text or chat messaging, screen sharing information, and possibly a composed video feed.

[0031] The PRSA 300 may be connected through a separate real-time media communications session with the sending participants. Thus, the receiving participants and the sending participants may be connected through a separate real-time media communication session. In the real-time media communications session established between the sending participants and the PRSA 300, the sending participants are sending media feeds and possibly supplementary information such as screen sharing information, or additional metadata with application information to the PRSA 300. The PRSA 300 also includes a supplementary information unit 310 which is responsible for obtaining, gathering, formatting and tracking a variety of supplementary information that could be rendered and presented to the real-time media communication participants (sending and/or receiving participants). To that end, the supplementary information unit 310 could include an attendee tracking unit 312 that tracks who was invited to attend the real-time media communications, who is currently attending the real-time media communications session, as well as other attendee-specific information, or any programmatically renderable information or media effect, or application part. For example, the attendee tracking unit 312 could track whether a particular attendee is receiving and using audio and video in the real-time media communications session, or only audio or a real-time processed insertion of information as an augmented reality component to the media information from the real-time media communications session.

[0032] The supplementary information unit 310 also may include a chat function unit 314 that allows senders and/or receiving participants to type text messages or questions that are seen by all real-time media communications participants or which are only seen by specific attendees. For example, the chat function unit 314 could allow a first participant to set up a private chat session with a second participant, in which case only the first and second participants would see the text messages passing back and forth between the two participants. Also, the chat function unit 314 could allow all media conference participants to type in questions, but where the questions are only seen by the senders, allowing the senders to control which questions are raised and answered during the media conference. The PRSA can then programmatically select any of the information of the chat available, either the information visible to all, or the one specific to some participants and render it at will, based on the specific use case designed by the PRSA.

[0033] The supplementary information unit 310 could further include a screen sharing presentation unit 316 that allows a sender and/or receiving participant to share what is shown on their computing device display screen with other video conference participants. The shared screen could appear in the center of the composed video feed or in a smaller window that appears in the composed video feed, or anywhere desired as per the PSRA programming, even including the mixture of additional media effects on it.

[0034] The supplementary information unit 310 could further include a supplementary rendering unit 318 that generates supplementary media feed data incorporating one or more items of supplementary information. The supplementary rendering unit 318 then sends the supplementary media feed data to the Composed Rendering Generation Unit 304 so that the

supplementary information can be incorporated into the composed media feed.

[0035] The above description only covers some of the elements that could be included in a supplementary information unit 310. A supplementary information unit 310 embodying the invention could include additional units to track and format other forms of supplementary information (e.g., an Augmented Reality Unit (320) that could be used among other things, to incorporate elements of AR/VR experiences to the composed media stream, e.g. a virtual meeting place with 3D avatars). It could also have a Media Effects Processing Unit (322) capable of adding special media effects to the composed media stream, for example, and not limited to, animating time-synced emoji reactions from participants in a video conference, or additional audio effects, etc. Likewise, a supplementary information unit 310 embodying the invention need not include all the items discussed above.

[0036] The PRSA 300 rendered composed media feed can be alternatively or complementary used as a feed for a recordation unit 328 that is responsible for creating a recording of a real-time media communications. In some embodiments, and most commonly, a separate recording API running on the same server 208 that is processing the various video feeds or in a different server may be responsible for generating a recording of a real-time media communications session. In that instance, the media feed recording unit could include an API interface 330 configured to interact with the recording API. In some embodiments (e.g. 300B), the API interface unit 330 could route the rendered composed media feed that includes supplementary information to the recording unit, by way of the Media Feed Receiving Unit (331 ), and sent from the Composed Rendered Media Sending Unit (326), so that the recording unit can make a recording of everything included in the rendered information by the PRSA, much richer than the bare combination of media

feeds from sending participants. In other embodiments (e.g. 300A), the media feed recordation unit 328 may itself be configured to make a recording of real-time media communications. In that instance, the Composed Rendered Media Feed Recordation Unit (328) can receive the composed media feed directly from the Composed Rendering Generation Unit (304) without the overhead of additional protocols & packaging required to send the media over a network. The API interface (330) provides an API which can be used to interface with the Recording Unit (332) to control the recording of the composed media. In some embodiments, a storage unit 334 of the video feed recordation unit 328 causes the rendered composition media feed to be recorded on a local data storage device of the server upon which the PRSA 300 is running. In other instances, the recording can be caused to be stored at a remote location, such as on a cloud storage or network unit, but not limited thereto.

[0037] The recording unit 328 may be running on the server upon which the PRSA 300 is running. Alternatively, the recording unit 328 could be running on a separate computer, server, cloud server, or a virtual computer or virtual server running in the cloud. Regardless, the recording unit is configured to record the audio of the rendered composed media feed along with the rendered video composed media feed, as opposed to a separate audio track that may be generated by the computer or server upon which the recording unit is running.

[0038] The Composed Rendering Generation Unit (304) can be implemented by means of a browser (or other software capable of rendering a web application at a given URL). The operation of the Composed Rendering Generation Unit (304) is controlled via the API Interface (302) which causes it to navigate to a URL at which to find the application capable of generating and controlling the composed rendering of the PRSA. This is the Program

Application (306). The same API interface then causes the Composed Rendered Media Sending Unit (326) to begin to capture the media data from the Composed Rendering Generation Unit (304). In some embodiments (e.g.

300A) media gets muxed and routed directly to the recordation unit (328) from the Composed Rendering Generation Unit (304) on the same machine. In other embodiments (e.g. 300B), the media gets muxed and prepared for sending over the network by means of the Composed Rendered Media Sending Unit (326) (adding the required encoding, protocols & packaging, including but not limited to, as an example, VP8, H264, OPUS, tcp/ip, udp, rtp, rtcp, etc.) to a remote recordation unit (328). In this embodiment (300B) the Remote Recordation Unit (328) contains a Media Feed Receiving Unit (331) which receives the possibly composed, encoded and packetized media feed being sent from the remote Composed Rendered Media Sending Unit (326), and proceeds to depacketize and decode and prepare as needed for the recording process (332) into to the Storage Unit (334). In another embodiment, instead of the Remote Recordation Unit, there might be in place broadcast unit of the composed media feed via RTMP(s) or distribute it as HLS or forward the stream via SIP Gateways or other RTC technology. The media generated by the Composed Rendered Media Sending Unit (326), may be also transmitted (e.g. 211) to Receiving endpoints (210, 212, 214, 216) and/or other functional units from a real-time media communications platform for further processing and/or use, such as SIP Gateways, or other RTC technology as depicted further in Figure 9 and Figure 10.

[0048] A method of providing Programmable Renderer services within a real-time media communications system or platform that would be performed by elements of a PRSA 300 is illustrated in Figure 5. The method 500 begins and proceeds to step 502 where a PRSA 300 is instantiated on a server. A software application to be executed by the PRSA is loaded and then run on the server at step 504 (in an embodiment of the invention, the application can be received through the API controlling the PRSA by means of a URL -Uniform Resource Locator-, aka web address). In step 506, a Senders Media Feeds Receiving Unit 308 of the PRSA 300 receives one or more sender media feeds of a real-time media communications session. In step 508, supplementary information and/or metadata, which may or may not be about or occurring within the real-time media session, is received in a supplementary information unit 310 of the PRSA 300. Abstract:
Abstract:

The present invention relates to a biosensor device contains five periodic layers of Si/BaF2 and a very thin defect layer of blood sample between two thin metal layers of Ag. The defect layer corresponds to different hemoglobin concentration related to anemia. Transfer matrix method is used to estimate transmission, reflection and absorption properties of the sensor. To analyse the transmittance characteristics, metal layer width, incident angle and defect layer, refractive index has been varied. Detailed analysis shows that the proposed device contains a quality factor of 990, and a sensitivity of 892.85 nm/RIU. The analysis shows that the proposed work gives maximum sensitivity, when the defective layer is placed between two metal layers.

[0003] Generally, a 1D photonic crystal (PC) based biosensor technique showed potential applications in identifying the numerous types of diseases in a human. Photonic crystals are used extensively in sensors, omnidirectional mirrors, dense wavelength division multiplexers (DWDM), optical filters, etc. and recently their applications in biosensing have attracted the attention of researchers.
[0004] Recently, a biosensor based on 2D PCs is also helpful and more sensitive for the diagnosis of various types of diseases in blood components, and it gives high accuracy, but it is not easy to fabricate. While 1D photonic crystals have a simple periodic structure, are easy to fabricate compared to 2D photonic crystals, and offer good sensitivity, Q-factor, delay time, and detection limit. 
[0005] The proposed device contains five periodic layers of Si/BaF2 and a thin layer (defect layer) of the blood sample which is sandwiched between two metal layers of Ag for the diagnosis of anemia in a human.
[0006] In the proposed invention we introduced two metal layers on both side of defect layer in a 1-D PC structure to improve sensitivity of device for anemia detection. The defect layer corresponds to the hemoglobin concentration at various stages of anemia. This structure is used to investigate the tunable characteristic with the variation of metal layer width, incident angle and defect layer refractive index.

The metal buffer layer, which is disposed adjacent to the waveguide layer, can carry out the total reflection and provide extra phase compensation of the total reflection at the same time. Accordingly, the propagation constant of the resonance wave would be much closer to the sensitivity of the phase, and the resonance electric field of the GMR biosensor would be much closer to the sensitive area. ABSTRACT METHOD AND SYSTEM FOR IMAGE PROCESSING The present disclosure provides a method and system for efficient real-time image processing on edge computing devices, particularly suited for resource-constrained environments. The method involves receiving an image comprising a plurality of pixels and identifying points of interest (POIs) through a pixel-wise iterative process using a predefined window (e.g., 3 x 3) and similarity criteria based on pixel value differences. Neighboring pixels are classified as leaf nodes or root nodes depending on whether the difference falls within a predefined threshold (e.g., 5 to 15), with root nodes representing POIs. The method generates a denoised output image while preserving essential features invariant to scale and rotation. TECHNICAL FIELD 
[0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of image processing, specifically to methods and systems for identifying points of interest within an image for enhanced image analysis. The disclosure focuses on edge computing-based image processing techniques that enable efficient and real-time processing of images, including denoising and feature extraction. 
BACKGROUND
[0002] In the field of image processing, several technical challenges persist, particularly when it comes to real-time processing, noise reduction and feature extraction in resource-constrained environments. Traditional methods for identifying points of interest in images often rely on computationally intensive algorithms that are unsuitable for edge devices with limited processing power and memory. These conventional approaches struggle with scalability, making them inefficient for processing high-resolution images or handling large datasets in real-time. Additionally, many existing techniques fail to preserve the original image context while effectively extracting meaningful features, which can lead to degraded performance in applications such as object detection, image segmentation, and augmented reality. Variations in image scale, rotation, and illumination further complicate the extraction of consistent features, affecting the robustness and accuracy of the processing methods. Moreover, standard denoising techniques may either over smooth the image, resulting in loss of important details, or inadequately remove noise, compromising the quality of the output. 
[0003] Conventional methods to address the technical problems of real-time image processing, feature extraction, and noise reduction include techniques such as Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT), Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF), and Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG). These methods, although effective in extracting features invariant to scale and rotation, are computationally intensive and unsuitable for resource-constrained environments like edge devices and embedded systems. Denoising techniques such as Gaussian filtering, median filtering, and bilateral filtering are commonly used but often lead to over smoothing, resulting in the loss of critical image details. Additionally, traditional convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and deep learning approaches require substantial computational power and large datasets, making them impractical for real-time applications on devices with limited processing capabilities. Parallel processing solutions, while available, often lack optimized algorithms tailored for graphical processing units (GPUs), leading to inefficient resource utilization. Furthermore, existing methods typically do not preserve the original representation of the image after feature extraction, compromising the context necessary for advanced processing tasks such as object detection, augmented reality, and robotic automation. The shortcomings of these conventional approaches include high computational cost, inability to operate efficiently under resource constraints, sensitivity to variations in scale and rotation, and inadequate preservation of image context, all of which hinder their effectiveness in real-time, edge-based image processing scenarios. As a result, there is a need for an improved method and system for image processing.

Abstract:
Abstract:

This invention relates to an automated fan safety system to prevent accidents and injuries from rotating blades of fans, ceiling fans and cutter machines. The system has proximity sensors like IR or capacitive sensors placed near the rotating blades. The sensors detect human hands or other objects around the blades. Upon detecting any danger the system applies mechanical brakes that kick in instantly to stop the blades from rotating thus preventing damage or injury to the user. The central control unit acts on the information received from the proximity sensors and activates the safety system in real time. It prevents the blades from stopping instantly if an interference is detected thus giving protection to those who may unknowingly come in contact with the fan or cutter machine. A user interface is also included in the system to give real time feedback on the safety system status like if the brakes were engaged and at what time the fan blades stopped due to detected interference. The system is pre-programmed to be easily installed in existing models of fans and cutting machines and is thus suitable for use in new and old appliances. It can also be used in homes, factories and industries where there is a hazard of rotating blades to users. Through the automated response to blade obstructions the system minimizes the chance of accidents and safety is guaranteed without human intervention. This invention gives a strong and scalable solution for blade safety. It addresses the emerging problem of blade appliance caused injuries and presents a unique way of eliminating such accidents through an active and automated system.

Description:1) Field of the Invention: -
The invention in the present case is about an automatic fan safety system to avoid accidents of rotating blades in electric fans, ceiling fans, and cutter machines. In particular, the invention encompasses a system that identifies human presence or interference around the blades and instantly activates mechanical brakes to prevent the fan blades from continuing rotation, thus avoiding finger cutting or other injuries due to high-speed blades. This safety system is most relevant to electric fans and cutting machines in domestic, factory, and other industrial premises, where accidents involving rotating blades are a major risk factor. 

2) Background of the Innovation: - Preamble to the Description

Currently, fan systems built for household and industrial environments have posed a considerable danger of injury because of the high-speed rotating blades. The common accidents widely occur in unprotected or exposed fan blades and include figure cutting, fractures, or hair entanglement. The necessity for a system that is intelligent and real-time such that it will give an immediate response to all sensing risks and avert accidents has therefore become vital. This invention includes mechanical braking, sensors for detection of obstacles close to the fan blades, and automatic control systems to deal with the concern. The system has: 

1. IR Sensors: Detects any things or body parts that are in near range of the rotating blades. 
2. Mechanical Braking Mechanism: Halts the fan blades almost instantaneously, immediately after identifying any obstacle. 
3. Control System: Monitors the input from sensor and activates the brake if it senses the possibility of collision. 
Safety Feature: Cessation of continuous operation until reset once obstruction is detected. 

3) Summary of the Invention: - 
This invention is about a mechanism that will help increase the safety of fans by implementing mechanical braking to halt the rotation of the blades whenever a risk of an injury such as figure cutting is detected. The system uses IR sensor technology that will assess the proximity of any object toward the rotating fan blades. 6. When a risk is identified, then the mechanical brake will disable the fan motor instantaneously to ensure safety at all levels of operation. This system provides the reset      functionality to resume safe operations as soon as the threat has subsided. This invention finds application in both domestic and industrial settings and conceives significantly enhanced safety levels.

   Relevance: Useful for understanding general shutoff systems, does not cover the instantaneous mechanical brake application of the present invention.

A block diagram captures the functioning of different elements within the system such as IR Sensor (1), Control Unit (2), Mechanical Brake (3) and Fan Motor (4). The IR sensor identifies an object in proximity to the fan blades and transmits a message to the control unit. At this point, the Control Unit decides if an emergency stop is warranted. If so, the system engages the mechanical brake, which locks the fan motor. After the obstruction is removed, the system goes back to normal operations.

This picture depicts the internal workings of Mechanical Brake (3) that gets activated when a certain obstacle is noticed. As part of an emergency stop signal from Control Unit (2), the rotating Fan Motor (4) must be instantly stopped to avoid hitting the brakes too hard.

2. Mechanical Brakes:

   Function: When an obstacle is detected, the sensor applies the mechanical brakes immediately, which halts the blade movement to prevent injuries.

   Function: Receives information from the proximity sensor and assumes command to engage the mechanical brakes whenever the system is endangered. Additionally, it controls the fan motor on off based on the sensor input.
