[0025] FIG. 1 illustrates a schematic block diagram of a handheld device 100 (hereinafter referred to as the device 100) for diagnosing plant diseases, according to an embodiment of the present invention. The device 100 may be adapted to capture images of a plant. The plant may be, but not limited to, a potato, a maize, a corn, a rice, a pulse, and so forth. Embodiments of the present invention are intended to include or otherwise cover any plant, including known, related art, and/or later developed technologies. Further, the device 100 may check for a presence for infestation in the plant. Upon detection of infestation, the device 100 may recommend treatment for the detected infestation. The device 100 may further render the recommended treatment in a language easily legible by farmers. Moreover, the recommended treatment may either be displayed on the device 100, or the device 100 may narrate/announce the recommended treatment. Furthermore, the device 100 may operate without an internet connection, being suitable for rural and remote agricultural areas.
[0026] In an embodiment of the present invention, the device 100 may be portable. The portability of the device 100 may enable a provision for being handheld. The device 100 may further feature means such as, straps, belts, bands, and so forth, for enhancing a security and portability of the device 100.
[0027] According to the embodiments of the present invention, the device 100 may incorporate non-limiting hardware components to enhance the processing speed and efficiency such as the device 100 may comprise an image capturing unit 102, an image acquisition unit 104, a processing unit 106, a computer vision algorithm 108, an offline database 110, a natural language processing (NLP) engine 112, and an output unit 114. In an embodiment of the present invention, the hardware components of the device 100 may be integrated with computer-executable instructions for overcoming the challenges and the limitations of the existing devices.
[0028] In an embodiment of the present invention, the image capturing unit 102 may be inbuilt and integrated in the device 100. The image capturing unit 102 may be adapted to capture plant images. The image capturing unit 102 may be, but not limited to, a camera, a video camera, and so forth. Embodiments of the present invention are intended to include or otherwise cover any type of the image capturing unit 102, including known, related art, and/or later developed technologies.
[0029] In an embodiment of the present invention, the image acquisition unit 104 may be inbuilt and integrated in the device 100. The image acquisition unit 104 may be adapted to receive the plant images captured by the image capturing unit 102.
[0030] In an embodiment of the present invention, the processing unit 106 may be in communication with the image acquisition unit 104. The processing unit 106 may be configured to analyze the received plant images. The analysis of the plant images may be carried out using the computer vision algorithm 108. The analysis of the plant images may locate an infested section in the plant.
[0031] The processing unit 106 may be configured to compare the infested section in the plant with a disease identification data stored in the offline database 110. The comparison may enable the processing unit 106 to prognose a disease in the plant. The offline database 110 may further store organic treatment recommendations for the corresponding prognosed disease. The treatment recommendations may be, but not limited to, verified organic farming solutions, bio-pesticides, composting techniques, companion planting suggestions, and so forth. Embodiments of the present invention are intended to include or otherwise cover any type of the treatment recommendations, including known, related art, and/or later developed technologies. The offline database 110 may further store region-specific disease profiles and organic treatment solutions to ensure location-relevant recommendations.
[0032] The processing unit 106 may be configured to deploy the natural language processing (NLP) engine 112 to process the treatment recommendations. The processing of the treatment recommendations may generate a context-specific information, relating to the treatment recommendations, in a farmer-friendly fashion. The generation of the context-specific information in the farmer-friendly fashion may include solutions such as, but not limited to, a use of local terminologies, a use of laymen language, a specification of brands, and so forth. Embodiments of the present invention are intended to include or otherwise cover any solutions for generation of the context-specific information in the farmer-friendly fashion, including known, related art, and/or later developed technologies.
[0033] The processing unit 106 may be configured to activate the output unit 114 for disbursing the generated context-specific information. The output unit 114 may be, but not limited to, a display screen for displaying the generated context-specific information, a speaker for narrating the generated context-specific information, and so forth. Embodiments of the present invention are intended to include or otherwise cover any type of the output unit 114, including known, related art, and/or later developed technologies. The processing unit 106 may further be configured to translate the generated context-specific information in a language of choice of the farmer.
[0034] In an exemplary embodiment of the present invention, the device 100 may be used for diagnosing diseases in pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) plants and providing organic treatment recommendations. A farmer may capture images of the millet crop using the image capturing unit, particularly focusing on symptomatic areas such as leaves, stems, and panicles. The device 100 may process these images using a computer vision algorithm to detect abnormalities, such as yellow streaks, white downy growth on the underside of leaves, and stunted panicle formation, which may be indicative of downy mildew (Sclerospora graminicola). 
[0035] The device 100 may then compare the detected symptoms with region-specific disease profiles stored in the offline database 110. For instance, in semi-arid regions, the database may identify pearl millet rust caused by Puccinia substriata based on observed reddish-brown pustules on leaves, while in humid regions, the device 100 may diagnose blast disease (Pyricularia grisea) from grayish lesions with dark margins on leaves and nodes. The offline database 110 also may include location-relevant organic treatment solutions. For downy mildew, the database may suggest treating seeds with hot water (50°C for 30 minutes) before sowing and applying Pseudomonas fluorescens as a biocontrol agent to infected plants. 
[0036] To ensure accessibility, the processing unit 106 may translate the generated context-specific information into a language of the farmer’s choice, making the recommendations easier to understand. The output unit 114 may display the recommendations on a screen, narrate them through a speaker, or use both for better comprehension. This feature ensures that even farmers with limited literacy may receive the guidance effectively. Since the device 100 operates without an internet connection, the device 100 may be suitable for farmers in rural and remote agricultural areas where connectivity is limited. This ensures uninterrupted access to disease diagnosis and treatment recommendations even in isolated regions. The treatment recommendations provided by the device 100 may be selected from verified organic farming solutions, including bio-pesticides, composting techniques, and companion planting suggestions. For example, in case of pearl millet blast disease, the device may recommend spraying a neem oil-based bio-pesticide and intercropping pearl millet with cowpea to naturally reduce disease incidence. For rust disease, the device may suggest applying compost tea spray to boost plant immunity and introducing marigold as a companion plant to deter pests.
[0037] By integrating computer vision, NLP-based translation, and offline disease profiling, the device 100 may provide an effective, farmer-friendly, and region-specific solution for millet disease management, promoting sustainable agricultural practices.

Description:BACKGROUND
Field of Invention
[001] Embodiments of the present invention generally relate to diagnosis of plant infestations and particularly to a handheld device for diagnosing plant diseases. 
Description of Related Art
[002] Agricultural productivity depends on maintaining plant health, yet plant diseases remain a significant challenge for farmers. Traditional methods for disease identification rely on expert knowledge, visual inspection, and laboratory analysis. These approaches often require substantial resources, making them inaccessible for small-scale farmers in remote areas. Early detection is essential for preventing large-scale crop damage, but farmers frequently lack reliable tools that enable timely diagnosis.
[003] Technological advancements have introduced digital solutions such as mobile applications and AI-driven models for plant disease identification. Some of these rely on image recognition algorithms that compare plant symptoms with known disease patterns. While such systems provide automated diagnosis, many require internet connectivity, limiting their usability in regions with poor network access. Furthermore, existing solutions primarily focus on disease detection, often neglecting the need for treatment recommendations tailored to specific farming conditions.
[004] Language and literacy barriers further complicate farmers' ability to access agricultural knowledge. Most available tools present information in text-based formats, making them difficult to use for individuals with limited literacy. Moreover, conventional treatment recommendations frequently emphasize chemical-based solutions, raising concerns about environmental sustainability and long-term soil health. A comprehensive system addressing offline accessibility, multilingual support, and sustainable treatment approaches remains absent in the existing technological landscape.
[005] There is thus a need for an improved and advanced handheld device for diagnosing plant diseases that can administer the aforementioned limitations in a more efficient manner.

The following specification particularly describes the invention and the manner in which it is performed:


Field of the Invention
The present invention relates to the field of thermoelectric cooling devices. More specifically, the present invention is a portable liquid cooling system designed for household and industrial applications. It utilizes a Peltier module-based thermoelectric cooling mechanism integrated with a uniquely engineered copper heat exchanger to achieve rapid and efficient cooling of liquids. 
Background of the Invention
Traditional methods of liquid cooling require significant time and energy consumption, presenting challenges for efficient and rapid cooling needs in both domestic and industrial applications. Existing cooling systems predominantly rely on air-based cooling mechanisms and fans, which transfer heat to the surrounding environment. This approach not only increases ambient temperatures but also impacts the surrounding area's thermal comfort.
The field of thermoelectric cooling, particularly using the Peltier effect, offers a promising alternative. The Peltier effect operates through the movement of electrons between P-type and N-type semiconductors, where one junction absorbs heat while the other releases it. This temperature differential can be effectively harnessed for cooling purposes when properly managed.
However, a critical challenge in Peltier-based cooling systems is managing the heat generated on the module's hot side. Without efficient heat dissipation, the accumulation of heat reduces the cooling efficiency and can lead to system performance degradation. Conventional heat management solutions often lack the necessary efficiency for rapid cooling applications.
Water, with its high thermal conductivity and specific heat capacity, presents an ideal medium for heat transfer in cooling applications. Despite this advantage, existing cooling systems have not fully optimized the integration of water-based heat exchange with Peltier cooling technology, particularly in portable applications.
There exists a need for a compact, efficient, and portable cooling solution that can rapidly cool liquids while effectively managing heat dissipation, making it suitable for both domestic use and specialized applications such as beverage cooling and medicine preservation
Objective of the Invention
The primary objective of the present invention is to develop a portable thermoelectric cooling kettle that enables rapid cooling of liquids using Peltier modules and an advanced heat exchanger system.
Another objective of the present invention is to efficiently manage heat dissipation through a uniquely engineered copper-based heat exchanger design, optimizing the cooling performance.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to create a sustainable and energy-efficient cooling solution that eliminates the need for traditional refrigerants or hazardous chemicals.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to provide a compact and portable design suitable for both domestic and industrial applications while maintaining high cooling efficiency.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to implement a multi-layered heat exchanger placement system that ensures optimal heat transfer from multiple Peltier modules.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to achieve rapid cooling through continuous water circulation using a mini submersible pump system integrated with the heat exchangers.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to develop a modular cooling system that allows easy replication and adaptation for various cooling applications.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to create a user-friendly cooling device that provides consistent and reliable performance without impacting ambient temperatures.
Yet another objective of the present invention is to design a scalable cooling solution that maintains operational stability through efficient heat removal from the Peltier module's N-side.

Summary of the present invention
The present invention addresses limitations of conventional cooling methods, such as reliance on fans, refrigerants, or prolonged cooling times, by providing a compact, energy-efficient, and environmentally friendly solution. The present invention a Portable Thermo Electric Cooling Kettle, is an innovative rapid liquid cooling solution utilizing nine strategically positioned Peltier modules (two on each side, one at bottom) operating at 12V/6A, combined with five uniquely engineered copper-based heat exchangers. [0003] Sustainable waste management and energy production are significant global challenges. Solid waste, including food waste, agricultural residues, and other biodegradable materials, often accumulates in landfills, releasing greenhouse gases that contribute to global warming. Traditional waste disposal methods are inefficient, energy-intensive, and fail to effectively utilize the gases produced, causing environmental harm. Pyrolysis offers a solution by thermally decomposing solid waste into valuable products such as biochar, biooil, and pyrogas. However, existing systems often rely on external fuel sources and struggle to fully harness the energy potential of the process, particularly given the variable flow and composition of pyrogas.
[0004] Non-patent literature IN202341010324 discloses a pyrolizer and a process of pyrolysis thereof. The process of pyrolysis comprises steps of initiating the process of pyrolysis, preheating and heating of the pyrolysis chambers, recirculating and condensing the flue gas and collecting the biochar. The pyrolizer comprises a feed hopper, a feed motor, a feed screw barrel, vertical drop chamber , pyrolysis chambers, variable pitch spiral driver, flue gas outlet, condenser unit, liquid sealed collection chamber, mounting frame, spiral driver motor, gas inlet tube, internal heating pipe, variable pitch spiral blade, gas path, gas sensors and temperature sensors. The pyrolizer enables uniform heat distribution with minimal heat loss for pyrolysis. However, the pyrolizer and the process of pyrolysis focuses on internal heating with heat supplied through internally heated pipes. The flue gas (equivalent to pyrogas) is recirculated through pipes to utilize only its sensible heat, without combusting the flue gas to harness its inherent energy without the recirculation of biooil. Further, the environmental impact of flue gas or its mitigation is not addressed. The flue gas is stated to be stored as biogas or used to produce bioelectricity. The pyrolizer and the process of pyrolysis highlights the ability to customize biochar properties but does not emphasize broader commercial applications or energy recovery benefits.

The waste is first sorted to remove recyclable inorganic materials of economic value (metals, glass) and other foreign materials that would be detrimental to the quality of the final product (stone, sand, construction debris, etc.). After size reduction, the waste is pyrolyzed at a temperature range of 250 to 600°F, in a high capacity, continuous mixer reactor, using in-situ viscous heating of the waste materials, to produce a highly uniform, granular synthetic product similar in energy content and handling characteristics to, but much cleaner burning than, natural coal. However, the process relies on in-situ viscous heating, reaching a maximum temperature of 316 °C. The lower temperature of 316 °C restricts the product’s utility primarily to energy applications, limiting its versatility and value. Further, mechanical mixing requires lower particle size feed material. The process primarily focuses on producing synthetic coal for energy use.

[0046] The present disclosure describes a system and method for energy recovery from solid waste conversion. The system introduces an innovative solution by incorporating a synchronized dual-fuel burner, a dynamic fuel-switching system, and a staged ignition and droplet combustion mechanism. This system uses its co-products, biooil and pyrogas, as energy sources to sustain the process itself, achieving a self-sustaining, zero-input energy cycle. Biooil serves as the primary fuel, with its flow rate automatically adjusted based on the flow and energy content of the pyrogas, which acts as the secondary fuel. The synchronized dual-fuel burner ensures seamless operation by maintaining efficient combustion as the energy contributions from pyrogas fluctuate. Additionally, the system regulates airflow based on the combined flow rates of biooil and pyrogas, optimizing the combustion process for maximum efficiency. The staged ignition and droplet combustion mechanism further simplifies biooil burning, enhancing thermal efficiency and operational reliability. This advanced system not only initiates the pyrolysis process using its own co-products but also sustains continuous operation without external energy inputs. By dynamically optimizing fuel and air flow, the system maximizes energy recovery, reduces environmental impact, and provides a highly efficient and eco-friendly solution for solid waste management.

[0050] In an embodiment, the system (102) may include a chamber (104). The chamber (104) may also be referred as a pyrolysis chamber (104) where conversion of solid waste may occur through a pyrolysis process. The chamber (104) may be a high-temperature, oxygen-limited environment where solid waste decomposes. Further, the system (102) may include an outer cylinder/metal cylinder (106), where the pyrolysis chamber (104) may be enclosed within an additional metal cylinder (106), creating an annular space between the chamber (104) and the metal cylinder (106). The bottom portion of the outer cylinder (106) may house a burner (108) for combustion of the biooil with the pyrogas. The annular space may serve as a conduit for exhaust gases generated during the pyrolysis, guiding them towards a chimney (110).
[0051] In an embodiment, insulation (140) may be included around the outer cylinder (106) to minimize heat loss, ensuring efficient thermal management and reducing energy consumption during the pyrolysis process. Further, a pyrovapor outlet pipe (112) may channel the pyrovapors generated during the pyrolysis of solid waste from the pyrolysis chamber (104) to a condenser (114).
[0052] In an embodiment, the condenser (114) may cool the vapors generated during the pyrolysis process. As the hot vapors pass through the condenser (114), the vapors may be cooled and transformed into liquid biooil. Further, once the vapors have condensed into liquid form, the biooil may be collected into a biooil collection tank (136). The collected biooil may be then be utilized as a primary fuel source for subsequent pyrolysis experiments.
[0053] In an embodiment, a non-return valve (118) may be configured with the system (102) to prevent the backflow of combustion air and exhaust gases into the condenser (114) and pyrolysis chamber (104), ensuring the system (102) operates safely and efficiently. The non-return valve (118) may be configured with the gas pump (138) to prevent the backflow of pyrogas to the pyrolysis chamber (104).

[0056] In an embodiment, a peristaltic pump (124) may deliver biooil from the biooil supply tank (116) to the burner (108). [0059] In an embodiment, the system (102) may be equipped with four thermocouples (132) strategically placed to monitor temperatures at critical points, the top, middle, and bottom of the burner, as well as a flame zone within the burner. [0060] In an embodiment, the system (102) may be designed to efficiently convert solid waste into biochar, biooil, and pyrogas through a controlled thermal decomposition process. The process may begin with loading solid waste into the pyrolysis chamber (104). This chamber (104) may be cylindrical in shape and designed to be removable, allowing for easy loading and unloading of materials. Once the chamber (104) is loaded, the chamber (104) may be securely placed within the outer cylinder (106) in the pyrolysis zone. The required amount of biooil is filled into the biooil supply tank (116), ensuring that the biooil is free from impurities. The process parameters, including target temperature, heating rate, residence time, biooil flow rate, air flow ratio, and oxygen concentration in the flue gas, may be received by the microcontroller for precise control.
[0061] In an embodiment, once all preparations are complete, the gas pump (138) may be switched on, and the burner (108) may be ignited to initiate the heating process in the combustion zone. As the biooil burns, the temperature inside the pyrolysis chamber (104) begins to rise. The system (102) may be equipped with four thermocouples that monitor the temperature at various points in the pyrolysis chamber. Once the internal temperature of the pyrolysis chamber (104) reaches the optimal range of 400-700 °C, pyrolysis of the solid waste may begin. During this process, the solid material in the pyrolysis chamber (104) may decompose in the oxygen-limited environment, producing three main products: biochar (solid), biooil (liquid), and pyrogas (gaseous). Biochar remains in the chamber and may be removed after the process is complete. Hot pyrovapors may be generated, containing both condensable and non-condensable fractions. The hot pyrovapors may be directed from the pyrolysis chamber through the pyrovapor outlet pipe to the condenser (114) in the condensation zone. In the condenser (114), the vapors may be cooled, causing the condensable fractions to condense into biooil. This biooil may be then collected in the biooil collection tank (136) as a fuel for subsequent pyrolysis operations. The non-condensable fraction of the vapors, known as pyrogas, may not condense in the condenser (114). Instead, the pyrogas may be drawn out by the gas pump (138) and directed through the pyrogas inlet pipe into the burner (108). This pyrogas may serve as an additional fuel source for the system, sustaining the pyrolysis process and reducing the need for external energy inputs. The exhaust gases produced during the combustion of biooil and pyrogas are expelled from through the chimney (110).
[0062] In an embodiment, the blower (120) may supply the necessary air for the combustion of biooil and pyrogas in the burner (108). The blower assembly (120), biooil pump assembly (124), and the microcontroller (130) may work together to regulate the biooil flow and airflow, based on feedback from the oxygen sensor (128) and the thermocouples (132). This may ensure optimal combustion conditions are maintained, contributing to the efficiency of the system (102). The non-return valve (118) may prevent the backflow of combustion air and exhaust gases into the pyrolysis chamber (104) and blower assembly (120), safeguarding the system (102) from potential hazards. At the end of the process, the system (102) may be powered down, and the pyrolysis chamber (104) may be allowed to cool to a safe temperature. Once cooled, the biochar may be retrieved from the pyrolysis chamber (104) for storage or further applications.
[0063] In an embodiment, the burner (108) may be configured as a synchronized dual-fuel burner capable of combusting both biooil and pyrogas as fuel sources. The combustion of biooil may follow a staged initiation and droplet combustion mechanism. Initially, a measured quantity of biooil may be introduced into the base of the burner (108) through the biooil inlet pipe and ignited. Combustion air may be supplied by the blower (120) through air inlet pipe and the combustion air may be distributed in the burner (108) by an air distributor. Once the initial biooil is ignited and burning, and the temperature within the burner (108) reaches a sufficient level, biooil from the biooil supply tank (116) may be introduced at a controlled flow rate in the form of droplets. As these biooil droplets enter the burner (108), the biooil droplets may evaporate, and the resulting vapors may combust, generating the necessary heat for the pyrolysis process. As the process continues, the pyrogas produced may enter the burner (108) through the pyrogas inlet pipe and may be mixed with the biooil vapors, providing supplementary heat and enhancing the overall efficiency. This synchronized dual-fuel burner (108) may ensure proper combustion of biooil while compensating for the heat contributions from pyrogas, thereby achieving efficient and consistent performance. The microcontroller (130) may maintain an optimal process condition by synchronizing the biooil and air flow rates with the pyrogas flow.
[0064] In an embodiment, the microcontroller (130) may synchronizes the biooil and air flows with the pyrogas flow to ensure efficient and controlled combustion, incorporating dynamic fuel switching that adjusts the biooil flow based on the energy contributions from pyrogas. The peristaltic pump (124) may supply biooil to the burner (108) at a user-defined flow rate, while the oil flow sensor (126) may monitor the actual flow rate and provides feedback to the microcontroller (130). Air may be supplied by the blower (120) to the burner (108), controlled to maintain the set air flow ratio with an air flow sensor measuring the air flow rate and sending real-time data to the microcontroller (130). A thermocouple installed in the burner (108) may continuously monitor the temperature and an oxygen sensor (128) in the chimney (110) may measure the oxygen concentration in the flue gas, both providing critical inputs to the microcontroller (130). A user may interacts with the system (102) through a digital display which shows set values such as temperature, heating rate, residence time, oil flow rate, air flow ratio, and oxygen concentration, as well as current process values like temperature, remaining time, oil flow rate, air flow rate, and oxygen concentration.

Description:TECHNICAL FIELD
[0001] The present disclosure relates to the field of gas turbine fuel injectors. More particularly, the present disclosure relates to a system for fuel-air mixer arrangement with a fuel flexibility mechanism of the injector assembly for lean-burn gas turbine combustion systems in aero engines and land-based gas turbine engines to enhance fuel delivery efficiency and reduce emissions.

BACKGROUND
[0002] Background description includes information that may be useful in understanding the present disclosure. It is not an admission that any of the information provided herein is prior art or relevant to the presently claimed disclosure, or that any publication specifically or implicitly referenced is prior art. 
[0003] Gas turbine engines are complex systems used for power generation and propulsion in various applications, including aero engines and land-based turbines. These engines operate by compressing air, mixing the air with fuel, and igniting the mixture to produce high-temperature, high-pressure gases that drive a turbine. Fuel injectors in these engines are important for atomizing and mixing fuel with air to ensure efficient combustion. In the case of fuel flexible gas turbine combustion system, the fuel injectors need to accommodate both liquid and gaseous fuels, such as Jet A1, methane, and hydrogen, to provide flexibility and efficiency in different operating conditions.
[0004] In the field of gas turbine engines, primary applicative goals include reducing emissions, improving fuel efficiency, and ensuring stable combustion across a wide range of operating conditions. Achieving these goals requires advanced combustion technologies that can handle both liquid and gaseous fuels while minimizing pollutants like NOx, CO, and CO2. Additionally, injectors need to be capable of operating efficiently at various power levels, from low-power conditions to high-power demands, to address the diverse needs of aero engines and localized power generation systems.
[0005] One of the main challenges in achieving these applicative goals is effective atomization and mixing fuel with air. This process plays a significant role in reducing emissions and improving combustion efficiency. However, existing fuel injector designs often struggle with issues such as coking of the fuel nozzle tip, inadequate atomization at low power conditions, and the need to prevent fuel impingement on injector surfaces. These challenges are exacerbated by the need to operate efficiently with both liquid and gaseous fuels, which have different atomization and mixing requirements.
[0006] Document US 6,418,726 B1 describes a method and apparatus for controlling combustor emissions in gas turbine engines. This document focuses on reducing emissions by optimizing the fuel-air mixing process. However, the document does not adequately address the challenges of operating with both liquid and gaseous fuels, nor does the document provide a comprehensive solution for preventing coking and ensuring efficient atomization across various power levels.
[0007] Document US 8,171,735 B2 discloses a mixer assembly for a gas turbine engine combustor, which aims to improve fuel atomization and mixing. While this document provides some advancements in mixer design, the disclosed invention falls short in addressing the specific needs of lean-burn systems that require flexibility in fuel type and operating conditions. The design does not fully prevent fuel impingement or coking, which are important for maintaining injector performance and longevity.
[0008] The specific problem addressed by then technological advancement is the need for a fuel injector design that can efficiently handle both liquid and gaseous fuels, prevent coking, and ensure effective atomization and mixing across a wide range of operating conditions. Existing solutions do not fully meet these requirements, highlighting the need for a novel approach to fuel injector design in gas turbine engines.
[0009]  There is, therefore, a need to overcome the above drawbacks, limitations, and shortcomings associated with the fuel flexible injector assembly that can minimize CO and NOx emissions, precise air distribution and advanced fuel atomization to enhance combustion uniformity, prevent localized hotspots, and present disclosure is disclosed.

[0011] An object of the present disclosure is to provide a system to achieve superior atomization and mix fuel with air, ensuring efficient combustion and reduced emissions across a wide range of operating conditions, from low power to high-power demands.

Abstract:
Abstract:

The invention is about a process to enhance a wet strength of papers that can be used as packaging material for tea bags. The invention provides a process for enhancing the wet tensile strength of paper products by utilizing bio-based epsilon polylysine in combination with oxidized cellulose fibers. Cellulose fibers are first oxidized using sodium periodate to form dialdehyde cellulose, which is then treated with epsilon polylysine and cationic starch to form modified cellulose fibers. The resulting paper exhibits significantly improved wet and dry tensile strength, making it suitable for applications such as wrapping paper, tea bags, facial tissues, and filter papers.

Description:FIELD OF THE INVENTION
The invention belongs to the technical field of paper packaging additives, and particularly relates to a process to enhance a wet strength of papers with bio-based wet strength additive for making papers. 

BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION
Wet strength is a very important property for many grades of paper that are exposed to water during use. Paper not treated for wet strength typically has 3-7% of its original dry strength available when tested while wet. It is also possible to further subdivide wet strength papers based on the permanence of their strength when wet. Paper which has not been treated typically loses its strength within seconds of being soaked in water, while with some wet strength chemicals the rate of wet strength loss during soaking is slowed. Such papers are said to possess temporary wet strength. Other chemicals provide a longer lasting effect and are said to impart permanent wet strength, even though the wet strength is not fully permanent.
Because of the need for paper products that retain some of their strength when soaked in water, chemical wet strength resins have been developed which produce paper products typically retaining 20-40% of their dry strength. In the paper industry, papers having wet tensile strengths of more than 15% of the original dry tensile strength are considered to be wet strength papers. In order to achieve wet strength, wet strength resins have been developed which are, in general, chemically reactive, water-soluble polymers that are added at the wet end of the paper machine. They are typically quite expensive and are prone to a host of problems. The first resins to become popular in use for improving wet strength were the aminoplast resins, urea-formaldehyde and melamine-formaldehyde. These resins are thermosetting and require heat and low pH to properly cure. They had adverse effects on brightness and absorbency, and the low pH was corrosive to the equipment. They have fallen out of common use because of environmental problems associated with their formaldehyde content/release. More recently, epoxidized polyamide resins (PAE) and glyoxalated polyacrylamide (GPAM) resins have been developed and have found generally good acceptance in the paper industry. They can be used in neutral or alkaline conditions and, while the epoxidized polyamide resins produce a permanent wet strength, the glyoxalated polyacrylamide resins provide only temporary wet strength, although some increase in dry strength is also achieved. 

Despite the significant advances that these resins represent, there are still a great many problems associated with their usage including high cost, limited storage life, expensive addition systems, pH control on the paper machine, curing time, and sensitivity to other chemicals. In addition, the epoxidized polyamide resins have environmental concerns because of the absorbable organic halogen (AOX) emissions, while the glyoxalated polyacrylamide resins are not suitable for all uses because of the temporary nature of their wet strength development.
The synthetic additives used in wet strength papers, however, are not easily bio-degradable, toxic, and have negative health implications when consumed directly and/or indirectly, thereby shifting the focus towards Bio based additives. PAE is the most commonly used wet strength additive in paper application. But, the precursors of PAE, epichlorohydrin is carcinogenic in nature and releases harmful chemicals like adsorbable organic halides (AOX), making the environment harmful when working with it. Hence there exist a need to focus on developing an environmentally friendly and food safe material for use as a wet strength additive in papermaking. Lately, several natural additives have been explored to provide wet strength properties to paper. These additives include modified starch, chitosan, wheat gluten and galactomannan. Permanent wet strength is achieved by crosslinking hydroxyl groups of cellulose with other functional groups. Chitosan was able to impart permanent wet strength in cellulose fibers because it was able to form amide linkage with cellulose fibers. However, it was less effective when compared to synthetic additives. 
Epsilon poly-l-lysine (EPL) is a naturally occurring bacterial cationic polymer with amine groups, which can react with aldehydes forming irreversible imine bonds by Schiff base reaction. Crosslinking aldehydes with amine groups results in forming permanent imine group called azomethine. Dialdehyde groups can be incorporated into cellulose fibers by oxidizing cellulose with periodate, which modifies the C2 and C3 hydroxyl groups forming dialdehyde cellulose (DAC).  EPL offers a promising substitute for traditional synthetic wet strength additives being used in making papers for various application and help in achieving the SDGs.
The invention is about a process employing a wet strength additive that is bio-based and more compatible to a wide variety of ecological considerations while still accomplishing the task of providing suitable wet strength in the finished product.

OBJECT OF THE INVENTION
The objective of the present invention is to provide a bio-based solution to the challenge of enhancing the wet strength of paper products, thereby replacing harmful synthetic additives. Specifically, the invention aims to provide a paper that meets the high wet strength requirements while avoiding carcinogenic, toxic, and environmentally harmful substances.

SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION
The invention is about a process to enhance a wet strength of papers that can be used as packaging material for various application. The cellulose fiber can be modified to provide the wet strength function of a product without the addition of any synthetic chemically reactive polymer. In accordance with this invention, the modification of cellulose fibers with polylysine results in significant improvements to the wet tensile strength and the dry tensile strength exhibited by paper sheets made with the treated fibers of this invention. The wet tensile strength: dry tensile strength ratio (sometimes referred to as the "wet over dry" ratio) can be increased without the addition of any other traditional wet strength agents.
The invention provides a process for enhancing the wet tensile strength of paper products by utilizing bio-based epsilon polylysine in combination with oxidized cellulose fibers. Cellulose fibers are first oxidized using sodium periodate to form dialdehyde cellulose, which is then treated with epsilon polylysine and cationic starch to form modified cellulose fibers. The resulting paper exhibits significantly improved wet and dry tensile strength, making it suitable for paper based applications such as tea bags, facial tissues, and filter papers.

DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF THE INVENTION
The wet tensile strength of the papers is enhanced for different applications such as tea bags, filter papers, facial tissues, etc. The cellulose fibers are oxidized using sodium periodate to form dialdehyde cellulose. The epsilon polylysine solution and cationic starch solution are prepared and Ioaded onto the dialdehyde cellulose to modify the fibers. The modified cellulose fibers are utilized to prepare handsheets of 30 g/m2. The dry and wet tensile strength of the handsheets increased with the reaction time of dialdehyde cellulose and epsilon polylysine. This indicates the use of the process for designing paper, replacing the synthetic additives to impart wet strength to the paper.
The invention provides a bio-based wet strength additive as an alternative replacing the usage of synthetic additives. Paper products such as tissues, tea bags, filter papers, etc., frequently come in contact with water; hence, wet strength of the material used for manufacturing plays a major role. However, the major problems to be addressed for the paper are: large amount of water absorption by paper due to its hydrophilic nature, use of synthetic additives in the existing solution, use of formaldehyde-based additives which can be carcinogenic, use of toxic and corrosive raw materials for synthesis of additives, lack of bio-based additives for making high wet-strength paper and a need for a simple processing technique to enhance the wet strength.
Formaldehyde and epichlorohydrine-based synthetic additives are most commonly used to increase the wet strength of the paper. However, they involve chemicals that are harmful to the environment. The formaldehyde is carcinogenic in nature and releases volatile organic compounds into the atmosphere. The utilization of such material for packaging food where food comes in direct contact with packaging material paper, for instance, in tea bags or food wrapping paper, could affect human health and issues of migration of packaging substance and micro plastic inhibition exist in the foods. Many industries are interested in including bio-based wet strength additives in papermaking, providing a safe solution for the high-wet strength papers. 
This invention aims to develop a high wet strength paper using bio-based epsilon polylysine as a wet strength additive. The paper thus produced can also be utilized for food contact applications due to the absence of carcinogenic and health-affecting compounds.
Sodium periodate is utilized to partially oxidize cellulose fibers into dialdehyde cellulose. Epsilon polylysine is a bio-based material that reduces the resistance to interaction with water by crosslinking with dialdehyde cellulose fibers. Moreover, the utilization of epsilon polylysine as a crosslinking agent of dialdehyde cellulose fibers can increase the wet strength of the paper along with reducing the reliability of carcinogenic and corrosive material being used in paper-making, especially that comes in contact with food such as tea bags, food wrapping paper, tissue paper, etc. 
The invention relates to a process of making cellulose fibers with increased wet strength that involves oxidation of cellulose fibers and grafting of oxidised cellulose fibers with polylysine. With regard to the oxidation reaction, there are a great many ways in which the chain units in cellulose can be oxidized. However, most oxidants are unspecific in their mode of attack. Suitable oxidants for purposes of this invention include, without limitation, sodium metaperiodate, sodium paraperiodate, periodic acid, sodium hypochlorite, hydrogen peroxide, ozone, potassium dichromate, potassium permanganate, and sodium chlorite. Periodate ions react with the cellulose without destroying its fibrous nature and result primarily in the oxidative scission of 1, 2 - diols to primarily produce dialdehyde oxycellulose under proper conditions. For this reason, the preferred oxidizing agents are the periodates, such as sodium metaperiodate (NaIO4). 

 The utilization of epsilon polylysine as a crosslinking agent of dialdehyde cellulose fibers can increase the wet strength of the paper along with reducing the reliability of carcinogenic and corrosive material being used in paper-making, especially that comes in contact with food. 

The pH of the oxidation reaction can preferably be from about 3 to about 4.6. At higher pH, the sodium metaperiodate is converted to insoluble paraperiodate.

When using sodium metaperiodate as the oxidation agent, the upper concentration of sodium metaperiodate is limited by its solubility in water, which is 14.44 grams per 100 milliliters at 25° C. The maximum concentration of sodium metaperiodate which can therefore be achieved is about 0.67M. On the other hand, at concentrations below about 0.005M the rate of reaction is too slow for the process to be economically feasible. Preferred concentrations are from about 0.01M to about 0.2M. At higher concentrations, although the reaction will proceed faster toward the desired degree of substitution, the shorter treatment time is likely to result in non-uniformity of the substitution.
The preparation method of a dialdehyde cellulose cross-linked with epsilon polylysine is characterized in that epsilon polylysine is grafted on the dialdehyde cellulose fibers.
Softwood bales were first disintegrated for 20 minutes (60,000 revolutions) in a disintegrator. The resulting pulp was then refined in a PFI mill at a consistency of 10 wt./vol.% (30g oven-dried pulp in 300 ml of water) until a freeness (°SR) of 40 was achieved. To modify the cellulose fibers, sodium periodate (NaIO4) was added at varying amounts of 0.1, 0.25, and 0.5 moles per mole of anhydride group in the cellulose fibers and the reaction was carried out for 30, 15, and 5 minutes respectively at a controlled pH of 3, adjusted with acetic acid, and conducted in a dark environment to prevent oxidation of NaIO4. The reaction was then stopped by adding ethylene glycol, after which the dialdehyde cellulose (DAC) was washed and the pH was adjusted to 9 by adding sodium hydroxide (NaOH). For each mole of DAC, 2 moles of epsilon poly-l-lysine (EPL) were dissolved in water to prepare an EPL solution, and the pH of this solution was also adjusted to 9 with NaOH. Simultaneously, a cationic starch (CS) solution was prepared by mixing 1 wt.% of CS with dry fiber mass in water, and the pH of this solution was adjusted to 9 using NaOH. The EPL and CS solutions were combined and added to the modified cellulose fibers. Handsheets with a grammage of 30 GSM were then prepared, pressed at 4 kgf/cm², and dried in an oven at 105°C overnight. The resulting EPL-grafted handsheets were used to produce high wet strength papers.
The oxidation/lysine crosslinking of cellulose results in significant improvements in the wet and dry tensile strength and provides high wet over dry tensile ratios for the cellulose pulp so treated. The wet and dry tensile strengths of cellulose pulp can be optionally further enhanced by refining the cellulose pulp prior to the oxidation/lysine cross-linking. Such refining also increases the wet over dry tensile ratio significantly. When used as a pre-treatment, refining serves to bring about external and internal fibrillation of the fibers. This increases the surface area of the fibers and also increases accessibility of the fibrils and cellulose chains to oxidation/crosslinking. These factors contribute to the observed increase in wet strengths which can be extremely useful in the manufacture of a wide variety of paper products such as tissue and towelling, board, tea bags, paper bags, wet wipes, and tissue wraps in personal care products and the like.
In the main embodiment of the invention the invention is about increasing the wet strength of the paper by using bio based additives such as epsilon polylysine. 
In an embodiment of the invention, the cellulose was oxidized using periodate to produce dialdehyde cellulose. 
In further embodiment, the dialdehyde cellulose is treated with a polylysine solution and cationic starch to produce modified cellulose fibers. 
In the next embodiment, the polylysine treated dialdehyde cellulose are used to produce paper with enhanced wet tensile strength. 
In the other embodiment, the process leads to a partial modification of cellulose into dialdehyde cellulose by reacting with sodium metaperiodate for a limited time period at a controlled acidic pH. 
In further embodiment, the action of metaperiodate with cellulose is halted by adding ethylene glycol. 
In still further embodiment, the treatment of cellulose fibers with sodium metaperiodate is carried out in dark conditions to prevent the oxidation of sodium metaperiodate. 
In the next embodiment, epsilon polylysine coupled with cationic starch is grafted on the surface of partially modified dialdehyde cellulose at an alkaline pH of approximately 9.
In the continued embodiment it leads to the formation of imine bonds between the amine groups of polylysine and aldehyde groups of dialdehyde cellulose. 
In the next embodiment, the percentage wet strength of the paper after crosslinking is 10-45%, as required by the wet strength papers. The tear strength index of the paper produced is in the range of 7 .5 to 9.5 mNm2/g. 

EXAMPLE
Softwood bales were disintegrated for 20 minutes (60,000 revolutions) in a disintegrator. Then the pulp was refined in a PFI mill at a pulp consistency of 10 wt./vol.% (30g oven-dried pulp in 300 ml water) until the °SR of 40 is reached. For every mole of anhydride group in cellulose fibers, 0.1, 0.25 and 0.5 moles of NaIO4 are added and the reaction was allowed to carryout for 30, 15 and 5 minutes at a controlled pH of 3 obtained by adding acetic acid. The whole reaction was carried out in a dark environment to prevent oxidation of NaIO4. The reaction was halted by adding ethylene glycol and the obtained DAC was washed followed by adjusting pH to 9 by adding NaOH. For every mole of DAC, 2 moles of EPL were dissolved in water to prepare an EPL solution and the pH of this solution was adjusted to 9 by adding NaOH. Simultaneously, cationic starch solution was prepared by loading 1 wt.% of CS on dry fiber mass in water and the pH of this solutions was also corrected to 9 using NaOH. The CS and EPL solution were mixed and loaded into the modified fibers followed by preparing handsheets of 30 GSM. The prepared handsheets were pressed at 4kgf/cm2 and then dried in an oven at 105? overnight. This process is illustrated in FIG. 1. 
The wet tensile strength of the resulting paper is found to be in the range of 10–45%, meeting the requirements for wet strength papers. The tear strength index of the paper is between 7.5 and 9.5 mNm²/g, further demonstrating its suitability for high-performance applications.
Example 
Bleached softwood pulp containing 20 weight percent hardwood pulp was used as the cellulose pulp. 100 grams of the pulp was oxidized by slurrying the pulp with 2000 milliliters of 0.05M sodium metaperiodate solution at ambient temperature for 1 to 6 hours. At the end of the oxidation reaction, the pulp was washed with distilled water to free it from unreacted reagents and by-products. For this washing step, water having a pH of 8 or greater should be avoided because dialdehyde oxycellulose degrades at alkaline pH. The significant product of the oxidation step was dialdehyde oxycellulose.
Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR)
The attenuated total reflection Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy was conducted on the prepared handsheets to determine the chemical composition using a Perkin Elmer, C91158 spectrophotometer. The spectra were taken with 4 cm-1 resolution and 
4000- 500 cm-1 wavelengths for every sample. All the spectra were baseline corrected and then normalized.
The addition of NaIO4 to cellulose results in oxidizing the anhydride groups in cellulose fibers forming a C=O linkage as observed at 1740 cm-1. This indicates the modification of cellulose into DAC. Further addition of EPL resulted in collapsing the carbonyl group (C=O), which can be directly correlated to the absence of peak at 1740 cm-1 for the EPL grafted fibers (DAC+EPL). Further, the broadening of peak at 1610 cm-1 indicates the formation of imine bonds between the amide groups of EPL and aldehydes of DAC, which are responsible for the enhanced wet strength of the paper. FTIR spectra of Neat, DAC and DAC+EPL papers are presented in FIG. 2.
Based on the visible modification in functional groups of papers, the possible mechanism of reaction between cellulose, NaIO4 and EPL is presented in FIG. 3. The cellulose fibers containing primary and secondary hydroxyl groups react with NaIO4 and are converted to dialdehyde cellulose. Further addition of EPL at an adjusted pH of 9 resulted in breakage of carbonyl groups and formation of imine bonds.
Grammage, thickness and porosity of prepared handsheets
The grammage of the prepared handsheets is maintained close to 30 g/m2 and the thickness of the handsheets along with mechanical properties is presented in Table 1. 
The dry and wet-tensile strength of the prepared handsheets were tested using a horizontal tensile tester (Frank PTI, Germany) following ISO 1924-2:2008 and IS-1060:2014. The dry-strength testing was performed on 15 mm wide strips, and the clamping length was set at 100 mm. Likewise, wet strength testing was done by dipping a 15 mm wide strip in distilled water for 1 minute, and the extra water was removed by manually rolling the strip placed in between the bloating papers. This wet sheet was then tested for tensile strength. Further % Wet strength was calculated using Eq 1. All the tests were carried out in triplicates

% Wet Strength =  (Wet Strength (N.m.g^(-1)))/(Dry Strength (N.m.g^(-1)))  ×100                   Eq 1
The dry and wet tensile strength of the neat paper without any modification is found to be 1149.473 N/m and 54.87 N/m respectively. For the paper to be considered to possess good wet strength, the % wet strength in terms of dry strength should be greater than or equal to 15%. For neat paper, the % wet strength is 4.77%, which is below 15% indicating poor wet strength. When the EPL is added to the modified cellulose fibers, whose modification time with NaIO4 is 5 minutes, the wet strength increased from 54.87 N/m for neat papers to 251.53 N/m, 356.72 N/m, and 433.93 N/m for 10, 25 and 50% modification. Abstract:
Abstract:

A force balance accelerometer (FBA) assembly (100) is disclosed for measuring low-frequency and low-amplitude accelerations with high sensitivity. The FBA assembly (100) includes a shaft (104) made of magnetically soft material, axially disposed within a hollow spool (122) fixed to a base (102). The shaft is biased to a central equilibrium position by a pair of compression springs (106) and is coupled to end caps (108) carrying movable capacitor plates (112). The plates face fixed capacitor plates (110) mounted on the spool (122) to form variable capacitors. Differential bias voltages (116,118) enable capacitive sensing of shaft-displacement due to external acceleration. A feedback circuit (200) including a differential amplifier (204), low-pass filter (206), and feedback stage (212) generates current in a coil (120) wrapped around the spool (122), producing an electromagnetic restoring force on the shaft. The feedback signal is proportional to the external acceleration acting on the base.

Description:TECHNICAL FIELD
[0001] The present disclosure relates to vibration sensing systems, specifically to a force balance accelerometer assembly for measuring low-frequency and low-amplitude accelerations with high sensitivity and electromagnetic feedback control.

BACKGROUND
[0002] Vibration sensing plays a critical role in understanding the dynamic behavior of mechanical and civil structures, enabling applications such as structural health monitoring, seismic activity detection, and inertial navigation. Accelerometers are widely used in such contexts to measure acceleration and derive insights into the structural or motion-related characteristics of the system. Among various types of accelerometers, force balance accelerometers (FBAs), also known as servo-accelerometers, are recognized for their high sensitivity and precision in measuring small amplitude and low-frequency vibrations.
[0003] A key objective in vibration measurement is to accurately detect subtle dynamic responses in the frequency range of 0–25 Hz and acceleration levels within ±5g, particularly for monitoring civil infrastructure or detecting ground motion during seismic events. Conventional accelerometers, including piezoelectric and MEMS-based sensors, often lack the resolution or stability needed for capturing such low-frequency, low-amplitude signals. Additionally, existing solutions may suffer from limitations in mechanical design, electromagnetic interference, or high manufacturing complexity, making them less suitable for continuous and reliable monitoring.
[0004] However, several challenges hinder the widespread adoption of high-sensitivity accelerometers in structural and geophysical applications. Most traditional FBA designs involve bulky assemblies and require complex integration of multiple subsystems such as spring-mass arrangements, capacitive pickups, and electromagnetic feedback units. Furthermore, precise alignment and damping are critical to prevent spurious oscillations and ensure signal fidelity. The need for compact, cost-effective, and robust designs remains largely unmet, especially for use in dense sensor networks deployed in field environments.
[0005] Existing force balance accelerometer configurations also tend to separate the spring-mass system and feedback mechanism into discrete units, increasing the size, complexity, and alignment sensitivity of the device. The fabrication of such assemblies often requires specialized machining and component tolerances, which drive up costs and hinder scalability. Additionally, traditional sensor housings may not effectively support modular assembly, rapid prototyping, or integration with modern digital signal conditioning electronics.
[0006] To overcome at least the aforementioned limitations, there is a need for an improved force balance accelerometer that offers an integrated and compact assembly of the mechanical sensing unit and electromagnetic feedback mechanism, facilitates easy fabrication and delivers high sensitivity, stability, and reliability for low-frequency vibration sensing applications.

OBJECTS OF THE PRESENT DISCLOSURE
[0007] A general object of the present disclosure is to provide a force balance accelerometer capable of accurately measuring low-frequency and low-amplitude accelerations for applications such as structural vibration monitoring and inertial navigation.
[0008] Another object of the present disclosure is to overcome the limitations of conventional accelerometers by offering a highly sensitive and stable sensor design that eliminates spurious oscillations and enhances measurement precision in the range of ±5g and frequencies up to 25 Hz.
[0009] Another object of the present disclosure is to provide a compact, cost-effective, and easily manufacturable accelerometer that integrates sensing and feedback mechanisms into a single unit, making it suitable for dense sensor networks and long-term deployment in field conditions.



SUMMARY
[0010] Aspects of the present disclosure generally relate to vibration sensing systems, specifically to a force balance accelerometer assembly for measuring low-frequency and low-amplitude accelerations with high sensitivity and electromagnetic feedback control.
[0011] In one aspect of the present disclosure, a force balance accelerometer (FBA) assembly is disclosed. The FBA assembly includes a base and a hollow spool fixed to the base. The FBA assembly also includes a shaft made of a magnetically soft material and slidably disposed along a longitudinal axis through a hollow space defined within the hollow spool. The FBA assembly also includes a pair of compression springs positioned between opposite end portions of the shaft and ends of the hollow spool, the compression springs configured to bias the shaft toward a central equilibrium position. The FBA assembly also includes a pair of end caps fixed to the longitudinal ends of the shaft, a set of movable capacitor plates mounted on the end caps, and a set of fixed capacitor plates mounted to the hollow spool. Herein, each fixed capacitor plate facing a corresponding movable capacitor plate across a dielectric gap to form a pair of variable capacitors. The FBA assembly also includes a coil wound around the hollow spool and configured to generate an electromagnetic field in response to an electrical signal. The FBA assembly also includes a first bias voltage and a second bias voltage supplies, of equal magnitude and opposite polarity, applied to the fixed capacitor plates. The FBA assembly also includes a feedback circuit configured to drive the coil with a feedback signal proportional to displacement of the shaft and restore the shaft to the equilibrium position. The displacement of the shaft due to external acceleration causes variation in the capacitance between the movable capacitor plates and the fixed capacitor plates. The feedback signal configured to restore the shaft to the equilibrium position is indicative of the external acceleration.

[0013] In one embodiment, the natural frequency of the shaft-spring system formed by the shaft and the compression springs is greater than 50 Hz.

The feedback circuit also includes a current driver within a feedback stage configured to supply current to the coil in accordance with the amplified or digitized signal.

[0025] Conventional accelerometers, including MEMS and piezoelectric types, often lack the sensitivity and resolution required for accurate measurement of low-frequency (0–25 Hz) and low-amplitude (±5g) vibrations, which are essential in structural health monitoring and seismic motion sensing. Existing force balance accelerometers offer higher precision but tend to be bulky, mechanically complex, and expensive to fabricate due to separate spring-mass and feedback components, requiring precise alignment and specialized assembly processes. Such limitations restrict their scalability, cost-effectiveness, and suitability for field deployment in dense sensor networks or low-cost installations..
[0026] The present disclosure addresses the limitations by providing a compact and integrated force balance accelerometer that combines a spring-mass sensing unit and an electromagnetic feedback system within a single housing. A magnetically soft shaft acts as the movable mass and is flanked by compression springs and end caps carrying movable capacitor plates, which interact with fixed plates mounted on a hollow spool. The relative displacement of the shaft alters the capacitance, which is processed by a feedback circuit that generates a current through a coil, producing an electromagnetic restoring force that returns the shaft to its equilibrium position. The closed-loop configuration eliminates spurious oscillations and enables precise acceleration sensing.
[0027] The technical effect of the invention lies in its ability to deliver high-resolution, low-noise acceleration measurements in a stable and compact design, with reduced dependency on mechanical alignment and complex assembly. The integration of sensing and actuation in a single unit improves structural robustness and ease of fabrication, including compatibility with 3D printing. The feedback-controlled force balance mechanism ensures linear response and accurate dynamic tracking of acceleration signals, making the system suitable for continuous structural monitoring, tilt sensing, and inertial navigation, particularly in applications requiring high sensitivity at low frequencies and amplitudes.

[0031] Referring to FIG. 1, an exemplary schematic drawing of a force balance accelerometer (FBA) assembly (100) is illustrated, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. The FBA assembly (100) may include a base (102), a shaft (104), a pair of compression springs (106), a set of end caps (108), a set of fixed capacitor plates (110), a set of movable capacitor plates (112), a pair of bias voltage sources (116, 118), a coil (120), and a hollow spool (122). 
[0032] In one embodiment, the hollow spool (122) may be wrapped with the coil (120) and fixed to the base (102). The base (102) may serve as the foundation of the FBA assembly (100) and provide a reference platform for mounting the other components. The shaft (104) may be slidably disposed along a longitudinal axis through a hollow space defined within the hollow spool (122). The shaft (104) may be made from a magnetically soft material, such as, but not limited to, low carbon mild steel, to facilitate rapid magnetization and demagnetization. In one embodiment, the shaft (104) may have a non-circular cross-section, such as a rectangular or square shape, but not limited thereto, to prevent rotational movement about the longitudinal axis and to maintain angular alignment. The internal geometry of the hollow spool (122) may conform to the cross-sectional shape of the shaft (104), thereby restricting angular play while allowing axial motion of the shaft in response to inertial forces. Longitudinal ends of the shaft (104) may be fixed to the end caps (108) (or flanges (108)).
[0033] In one embodiment, each of the opposite longitudinal end portions of the shaft (104) may be inserted concentrically into a corresponding compression spring (106), such that the shaft (104) extends through the central axis of both springs. The compression springs (106) may be positioned between ends of the hollow spool (122) and the end caps (108) (or flanges). Such configuration may allow the shaft (104) to move freely along a longitudinal axis of the shaft (104) in response to external acceleration, while the compression springs (106) exert equal and opposite restoring forces to bias the shaft (104) toward a central equilibrium position. The geometry and stiffness of the springs, in conjunction with the mass of the shaft (104), may be selected to achieve a natural frequency of the sensor greater than 50 Hz. The geometry and stiffness of the springs ensures high sensitivity in detecting low-frequency, low-amplitude vibrations with minimal signal distortion, making the assembly suitable for structural health monitoring and precision inertial measurements.
[0034] Further, each of the set of movable capacitor plates (112) may be mounted on the end caps (108) rigidly coupled to the shaft (104), such that the movable plates translate along with the shaft during longitudinal (or axial) motion. The corresponding set of fixed capacitor plates (110) may be mounted to walls of the hollow spool (122) or associated structural elements. Each movable capacitor plate (112) may be positioned to face a corresponding fixed capacitor plate (110) with a natural dielectric gap (such as air, but not limited thereto) in between, thereby forming two variable capacitors. A first bias voltage supply (116) and a second bias voltage supply (118), equal in magnitude and opposite in polarity (e.g., +12 VDC and -12 VDC), may be applied to the fixed plates to establish an electrostatic potential across each capacitor. The capacitance of each pair varies inversely with the axial displacement of the shaft, enabling differential capacitive sensing of the shaft position relative to the base (102).
[0035] In one embodiment, the force balance accelerometer (FBA) assembly (100) may function by sensing axial acceleration through displacement of the shaft (104) relative to the base (102). When the base (102) experiences acceleration, the inertia of the shaft (104) may cause the shaft (104) to move against the biasing force of the compression springs (106), resulting in a change in the distance between the movable capacitor plates (112) and the fixed capacitor plates (110). The displacement may modify the capacitance between the opposing capacitor plates, producing a differential capacitive signal that may be proportional to the relative motion of the shaft (104). To restore the shaft (104) to the equilibrium (null) position and maintain dynamic balance, an electromagnetic force is generated by passing current through the coil (120) wound around the hollow spool (122). The magnetic field induced in the coil (120) may magnetize the shaft (104), thereby exerting a corrective force that counteracts the inertial displacement. The current required to maintain the shaft at or near the null position is indicative of the external acceleration acting on the base (102), enabling precise measurement of low-frequency and low-amplitude vibrations.
[0036] Referring to FIG. 2, an exemplary schematic block diagram of a signal conditioning and feedback control circuit (200) (may also be referred to as feedback circuit (200)) for the force balance accelerometer (FBA) assembly (100) is illustrated, in accordance with one or more embodiments of the present disclosure. The signal processing and feedback circuit (200) may include a variable capacitance accelerometer (202), a differential amplifier (204), a low-pass filter (206), an analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion block (208), a data storage unit (210), and a feedback stage (212). The fixed capacitor plates (110) may be electrically connected to a first bias voltage supply (116) and a second bias voltage supply (118), equal in magnitude and opposite in polarity, to enable differential capacitive sensing.
[0037] In one embodiment, the variable capacitance accelerometer (202) may include the physical assembly as described in FIG. 1. The physical assembly may provide two variable capacitors formed between the movable capacitor plates (112) and the fixed capacitor plates (110). The relative displacement of the shaft (104), caused by inertial motion due to acceleration of the base (102), leads to an imbalance in the two capacitances, which is detected as a differential voltage signal.
[0038] The differential output from the variable capacitance accelerometer (202) may be fed into the differential amplifier (204). The differential amplifier (204) may amplify the small voltage difference arising from capacitance variation, which is proportional to the displacement of the shaft (104). The amplified voltage output serves as an analog representation of the sensed acceleration.
[0039] In one exemplary embodiment, the differential amplifier (204) may be configured to receive input signals from the movable capacitor plates (112) associated with the shaft (104), and to amplify the voltage difference resulting from the capacitive imbalance between the movable capacitor plates (112) and the fixed capacitor plates (110). The differential amplifier (204) may include high-input-impedance operational amplifiers arranged in a differential configuration to ensure accurate amplification of small signal variations corresponding to low-level acceleration-induced displacements. The output of the differential amplifier (204) may represent a proportional analog voltage signal corresponding to the relative displacement of the shaft (104) from the equilibrium position. In some embodiments, the differential amplifier (204) may incorporate common-mode rejection capabilities to suppress noise and interference, thereby enhancing signal fidelity. The amplified output may be further processed by a low-pass filter (206) before being digitized for storage or feedback control operations.
[0040] The amplified analog signal may then be passed through a low-pass filter (206) to eliminate high-frequency noise or transient spikes not representative of structural vibration or tilt-related acceleration. In one example, an RC-type low-pass filter may be employed to preserve the integrity of low-frequency signals, which are characteristic of structural vibrations typically below 25 Hz.
[0041] In one exemplary embodiment, the low-pass filter (206) may include, but is not limited to, passive RC filter circuits, active filter configurations using operational amplifiers, or digital filtering algorithms implemented through a microcontroller or digital signal processor. The cutoff frequency of the low-pass filter (206) may be selected based on the target frequency range of interest, such as 0–25 Hz, to preserve relevant signal content while eliminating unwanted high-frequency transients or jitter. In certain embodiments, the filter may be implemented as a multi-stage or second-order filter to achieve sharper roll-off characteristics. The filtered output may then be forwarded to an analog-to-digital converter (208) for subsequent digital processing and storage.
[0042] The filtered analog signal may then be digitized using an analog-to-digital (A/D) conversion module (208). The A/D conversion (208) may enable real-time sampling and digital processing of the acceleration signal. In one embodiment, a microcontroller or digital signal processor (DSP) may be used for high-resolution conversion and further signal computation. 
[0043] In one exemplary embodiment, the analog-to-digital converter (208) may be configured to receive the filtered analog signal from the low-pass filter (206) and convert the filtered analog signal into a corresponding digital signal suitable for processing, storage, or transmission. The analog-to-digital converter (208) may include, but is not limited to, successive approximation register (SAR), sigma-delta (S?), or flash-type ADC architectures, depending on the resolution, accuracy, and sampling rate requirements of the application. In certain embodiments, the analog-to-digital converter (208) may be integrated within a microcontroller or digital signal processor (DSP) to enable compact system design. The resolution of the converter may range from 12 to 24 bits to ensure adequate precision in capturing low-amplitude vibration signals. The digitized output from the analog-to-digital converter (208) may be transmitted to the storage unit (210) and/or utilized by the feedback stage (212) to maintain the shaft (104) in its null position during dynamic operation.
[0044] The digital output from the A/D converter may be stored in a data storage unit (210), which may include onboard memory, external storage media, or a remote data acquisition system. The stored data may be used for continuous monitoring, offline analysis, or fault detection in structural health monitoring or inertial navigation systems. Simultaneously, the amplified analog signal from the differential amplifier (204), or digitally processed equivalent of the amplified analog signal, may be routed to via the feedback stage (212). The feedback stage (212) may include a power amplifier and a current driver configured to supply current to the coil (120) wrapped around the hollow spool (122). The resulting electromagnetic field may magnetically interact with the shaft (104), generating a restoring force that re-centers the shaft (104) to the equilibrium (null) position. The closed-loop feedback ensures that the shaft remains nearly stationary with respect to the base, and the feedback signal required to maintain this condition becomes a direct measure of the external acceleration acting on the sensor.
[0045] In one exemplary embodiment, the storage unit (210) may include, but is not limited to, any form of non-volatile memory such as flash memory, EEPROM, solid-state drives (SSD), or other forms of integrated digital memory circuits. In certain embodiments, the storage unit (210) may be integrated within a microcontroller or a digital signal processor (DSP), allowing for compact implementation of the signal conditioning and data logging subsystems. The stored data may represent time-stamped acceleration values corresponding to the output of the force balance accelerometer (100), and may be periodically offloaded to an external computing device or monitoring system for further analysis. In some implementations, the storage unit (210) may also be configured to retain calibration data, threshold levels, or system diagnostics to support continuous monitoring and long-term field deployment of the sensor.
[0046] In one exemplary embodiment, a current control mechanism may be provided to regulate the magnitude of current supplied to the coil (120) based on the output of the feedback stage (212). The current driver may be configured to respond proportionally to the voltage signal generated by the differential amplifier (204) or the digital signal from the analog-to-digital converter (208), thereby controlling the electromagnetic force acting on the shaft (104). In some embodiments, pulse-width modulation (PWM) or analog current regulation may be used to optimize power efficiency while maintaining rapid response to dynamic acceleration inputs. The tuning may ensure precise rebalancing of the shaft (104) and minimizes oscillations.
[0047] In one exemplary embodiment, the shaft (104) may be made from a magnetically soft material, such as low-carbon mild steel, to allow rapid magnetization and demagnetization under the influence of the magnetic field generated by the coil (120). The hollow spool (122) and base (102) may be constructed from non-magnetic materials, such as polymer composites or aluminum alloys, to avoid undesired magnetic interference and to facilitate lightweight construction. 
[0048] In one exemplary embodiment, the movable capacitor plates (112) may be configured with extended flanged arms or curved profiles to increase air passive damping during motion of the shaft (104). The passive damping helps to suppress spurious oscillations and stabilizes the sensor response in dynamic environments. Such configuration may also serve to enhance alignment of the plates with respect to the fixed capacitor plates (110), ensuring a consistent dielectric gap and linear capacitive response. The added damping improves signal fidelity, particularly in low-frequency vibration measurements.
